It's strange to think, but I have no doubt he has entirely forgotten Ellen Dean, and forgotten that he once meant more than the whole world to her, and she to him!

Here the housekeeper happened to glance at the clock over the fireplace and was astonished to see the minute hand marking half past one. She refused to stay another second. In truth, I too felt inclined to postpone the rest of her story. Now that she has disappeared to bed and I have reflected for another hour or two, I shall gather the courage to follow her example, despite the aching heaviness in my head and limbs.

chapters.title: Chapter X
paragraphs: What a charming beginning to a hermit's life! Four weeks of suffering, tossing in bed and sickness! Oh, these bleak winds, bitter northern skies, impassable roads and slow country doctors! And oh, this scarcity of human faces! Worse still, Kenneth's dreadful suggestion that I should not expect to go outdoors before spring!

Mr. Heathcliff has just honoured me with a visit. A week or so ago he sent me two grouse, the last of the season. Scoundrel! He bears some responsibility for my illness, and I was very tempted to tell him so. But alas! How could I offend someone kind enough to sit by my bed for a full hour and talk about something besides pills, medicines, blisters and leeches? Just now I am fairly comfortable. Too weak to read, I still feel capable of enjoying something interesting. Why not send for Mrs. Dean to finish her story? I remember the main events up to the point she reached. Yes: her hero had run away and nothing had been heard of him for three years; her heroine had married. I'll ring: she'll be delighted to find me able to talk cheerfully. Mrs. Dean came.
“Twenty minutes until your next medicine, sir,” she began.
“Away with it, away!” I replied. “What I want is—”
“The doctor says you're to stop taking the powders.”

“Gladly! Don't interrupt me. Come and sit here. Keep your hands away from that bitter army of bottles. Take your knitting out of your pocket—good. Now go on with Mr. Heathcliff's history from where you stopped until the present. Did he finish his education on the Continent and return a gentleman? Or get a subsidised place at college, or escape to America and win honours by shedding the blood of his adopted country? Or make his fortune faster by robbing travellers on English roads?”

“Perhaps he tried a little of all those professions, Mr. Lockwood, but I can't vouch for any. As I told you, I don't know how he made his money. Nor do I know how he lifted his mind out of the savage ignorance it had sunk into. But with your permission I'll tell it in my own way, if you think it will entertain you rather than tire you. Are you better this morning?”
“Much better.”
“I'm glad to hear it.”

I brought Miss Catherine and myself to Thrushcross Grange, and, to my pleasant surprise, she behaved far better than I had dared hope. She seemed almost excessively fond of Mr. Linton and showed his sister plenty of affection too. Certainly both took great care of her comfort. The thorn did not bend towards the honeysuckles: the honeysuckles wound themselves round the thorn. Nobody met halfway; one stood straight while the others yielded. And who _can_ be unkind and cross when met with neither resistance nor indifference? I noticed that Mr. Edgar had a deeply rooted dread of disturbing her temper. He concealed it from her; but whenever I answered sharply, or another servant looked displeased at one of her imperious orders, he revealed his distress with a frown he never wore on his own behalf. Often he reprimanded me severely for my impertinence, declaring that a knife could not hurt him more than seeing his wife upset. To avoid distressing a kind master, I learned to be less touchy. For six months the gunpowder lay as harmless as sand, because no flame came near enough to set it off. Catherine occasionally fell into gloomy silences; her husband respected them with sympathetic silence of his own, attributing them to a change in her constitution after that dangerous illness, since she had never been depressed before. When her sunshine returned, his answered it. I think I can say they enjoyed a deep and growing happiness.

It ended. Well, in the long run we _must_ look after ourselves: the gentle and generous are selfish more justifiably than the domineering, that is all. It ended when circumstances made each feel that their own interest did not come first in the other's thoughts. One mild September evening I was returning from the garden with a heavy basket of apples I had picked. Dusk had fallen, and the moon peered over the high courtyard wall, leaving vague shadows lurking in the corners of the building's many projecting parts. I put the basket on the steps by the kitchen door and paused to rest, breathing a little more of the soft, sweet air. With my eyes on the moon and my back to the entrance, I heard a voice behind me say, “Nelly, is that you?”

The voice was deep and its tone unfamiliar, but something about the way it spoke my name was familiar. I turned apprehensively to see who had spoken, for the doors were shut and I had seen nobody as I approached the steps. Something moved in the porch. Coming closer, I made out a tall man in dark clothes, with a dark face and hair. He leaned against its side, fingers resting on the latch as though he meant to open the door himself. “Who can that be?” I thought. “Mr. Earnshaw? Oh, no! His voice sounds nothing like this.”
“I've been waiting here an hour,” he continued as I went on staring. “All that time everything around has been as quiet as death. I didn't dare go in. Don't you know me? Look, I'm no stranger!”
A moonbeam lit his features: sallow cheeks half hidden by black whiskers, a frowning brow, and unusual, deep-set eyes. I remembered those eyes.
“What!” I cried, raising my hands in amazement, uncertain whether this visitor belonged to the living world. “What! You've returned? Is it you? Really you?”

“Yes, Heathcliff,” he replied, glancing past me at the windows, which reflected twenty glittering moons but no light from inside. “Are they home? Where is she? Nelly, you aren't pleased! Don't be so upset. Is she here? Speak! I want just one word with her—with your mistress. Go and say someone from Gimmerton wants to see her.”

“How will she bear it?” I exclaimed. “What will she do? I'm bewildered by the surprise—it will drive her out of her senses! And you _are_ Heathcliff! But how changed! No, I can't understand it. Have you been a soldier?”
“Take my message,” he interrupted impatiently. “I'm in hell until you do!”

He raised the latch and I went in, but on reaching the parlour where Mr. and Mrs. Linton sat, I could not bring myself to continue. Finally I decided to use the excuse of asking whether they wanted the candles lit, and opened the door.

They were sitting together in a window opened back against the wall. Beyond the garden trees and the wild green park it showed Gimmerton valley, with a long ribbon of mist winding almost to its head. As you may have noticed, just beyond the chapel the drain from the marshes joins a stream that follows the curve of the valley. Wuthering Heights rose above the silvery vapour, though our old house, dipping down a little on the far side, could not be seen. The room, the two people in it, and the view before them all looked wonderfully peaceful. I dreaded carrying out my errand and, after asking about the candles, was actually leaving without delivering it. Then, feeling how foolish I was, I turned back and murmured, “Someone from Gimmerton would like to see you, ma'am.”
“What does this person want?” Mrs. Linton asked.
“I didn't ask him,” I replied.
“Well, draw the curtains, Nelly,” she said, “and bring the tea upstairs. I'll be back in a moment.”
She left the room, and Mr. Edgar casually asked who had called.
“Someone the mistress isn't expecting,” I replied. “Heathcliff—you remember him, sir—the one who lived at Mr. Earnshaw's.”
“What! That gypsy—the ploughboy?” he exclaimed. “Why didn't you tell Catherine who it was?”
“Hush! Don't call him those names, master,” I said. “Hearing that would hurt her badly. His running away almost broke her heart. I expect she'll see his return as a reason for celebration.”

Mr. Linton crossed to another window overlooking the courtyard, unfastened it and leaned outside. They must have been below, for he quickly called, “Don't stand there, darling! If it's someone important, bring him in.” Soon I heard the latch click and Catherine rushed upstairs, wild and breathless, too excited even to look happy. Her face might sooner have made you suppose a terrible disaster had happened.
“Oh, Edgar, Edgar!” she gasped, throwing her arms around his neck. “Oh, my darling Edgar! Heathcliff's back—he really is!” And her embrace tightened into a squeeze.
“Well, well,” her husband exclaimed irritably, “don't strangle me over it! I never thought him such a wonderful treasure. There's no need to go wild!”
“I know you didn't like him,” she answered, restraining her delight a little. “But you must be friends now, for my sake. Shall I ask him upstairs?”
“Here?” he asked. “Into this parlour?”
“Where else would he go?” she asked.
Looking annoyed, he suggested the kitchen would suit him better. Mrs. Linton regarded him with an odd expression, half angry and half amused by his fastidiousness.

“No,” she said after a pause. “I can't sit in the kitchen. Lay two tables here, Ellen: one for your master and Miss Isabella, since they're gentlefolk, and another for Heathcliff and me, since we're lower class. Will that please you, darling? Or should I have a fire lit somewhere else? If so, give the orders. I'll run down and make sure of my guest. I'm afraid this happiness is too great to be real!”
She was about to rush out again when Edgar stopped her.

“_You_ ask him to come upstairs,” he told me. “And Catherine, try to be happy without making yourself absurd. The entire household needn't see you welcoming a runaway servant as though he were your brother.”

I went downstairs and found Heathcliff in the porch, clearly waiting for an invitation to enter. He followed without unnecessary words, and I brought him before the master and mistress, whose flushed faces showed they had been talking heatedly. But a different feeling lit the lady's cheeks when her friend appeared. She sprang up, took both his hands and led him to Linton, then caught Linton's unwilling fingers and pressed them into Heathcliff's. Now that fire and candlelight showed him fully, his transformation amazed me more than ever. He had become a tall, strong, well-built man beside whom my master looked slender and boyish. His erect bearing suggested time in the army. His expression and sharply defined features made his face look much older than Mr. Linton's; it looked intelligent and bore none of its old degradation. A half-tamed fierceness still lurked beneath the lowered brows and in eyes burning darkly, but he kept it controlled. His manner was even dignified, entirely free of coarseness, though too severe to be graceful. My master was as astonished as I, perhaps more so. For a minute he could not find a way to address the “ploughboy.” Heathcliff released his delicate hand and looked at him coolly until he chose to speak.
“Please sit, sir,” he said at last. “Remembering old times, Mrs. Linton wishes me to welcome you warmly. Naturally, anything that pleases her pleases me.”
“And me too,” Heathcliff answered, “especially when I have some share in causing it. I'll gladly stay an hour or two.”

He sat opposite Catherine, who watched him as though afraid he would vanish if she looked away. He rarely looked directly at her; an occasional swift glance was enough, but each returned with growing confidence the undisguised delight he drew from her eyes. Their shared happiness occupied them too completely for embarrassment. Mr. Edgar was different: sheer annoyance made him pale, and it reached its height when his wife stood up, crossed the rug and seized Heathcliff's hands again, laughing as though beside herself.

“Tomorrow I'll think it was a dream!” she cried. “I won't believe I've seen you, touched you and spoken to you again. Yet, cruel Heathcliff! You don't deserve such a welcome. Three years away without a word, and never a thought for me!”

“Rather more thought than you've spared me,” he murmured. “I only recently heard of your marriage, Cathy. While I waited downstairs in the yard, I planned to catch one glimpse of your face, perhaps a surprised look and some pretence of pleasure; then settle with Hindley, and spare the law its work by executing myself. Your welcome has driven those thoughts away. But don't meet me differently next time! No, you won't send me away again. Were you really sorry for me? Well, you had reason. I've fought through a bitter life since I last heard your voice. You must forgive me, because all my struggle was for you!”

“Catherine, please come to the table unless you want cold tea,” Linton interrupted, trying to maintain his usual voice and a proper degree of courtesy. “Wherever Mr. Heathcliff is staying tonight, he'll have a long walk, and I'm thirsty.”

She sat down before the tea urn, and Miss Isabella came at the bell. After drawing up their chairs I left them. The meal scarcely lasted ten minutes. Catherine's cup was never filled; she could neither eat nor drink. Edgar spilled tea into his saucer and swallowed hardly anything. Their visitor stayed no more than another hour that evening. As he left, I asked whether he was going to Gimmerton.
“No, Wuthering Heights,” he replied. “Mr. Earnshaw invited me when I visited him this morning.”

Mr. Earnshaw had invited _him_! And _he_ had visited Mr. Earnshaw! I pondered those words uneasily after he left. Was he becoming a hypocrite, returning here to cause trouble under a disguise? Deep down, I had a foreboding that it would have been better if he had stayed away.
Around the middle of the night Mrs. Linton slipped into my room, sat on the edge of my bed and pulled my hair, waking me from my first sleep.

“I can't rest, Ellen,” she said in apology, “and I want some living creature to share my happiness! Edgar's sulking because I'm pleased about something that doesn't interest him. He won't speak except to say foolish, peevish things, and he called me cruel and selfish for wanting to talk when he felt so ill and sleepy. He always manages to be ill at the slightest displeasure! I said a few good things about Heathcliff, and he started crying, either from a headache or a stab of jealousy, so I got up and left him.”

“What good does praising Heathcliff to him do?” I answered. “They disliked each other as boys, and Heathcliff would hate hearing praise of him just as much. That's human nature. Leave Mr. Linton alone on the subject, unless you want an open quarrel between them.”

“But doesn't it show great weakness?” she went on. “I'm not jealous. Isabella's shining yellow hair and white skin, her delicate elegance, and all the family's love for her never hurt my feelings. Even you, Nelly, take Isabella's side at once when we quarrel, and I give way like a foolish mother, call her a darling and flatter her back into a good temper. Her brother likes seeing us affectionate, and that pleases me. But they're much alike: spoiled children who think the world was made for their convenience. Though I indulge them both, I still believe a sharp lesson would do them good.”

“You're mistaken, Mrs. Linton,” I said. “They're the ones indulging you. I know what would happen if they stopped. It's easy to tolerate their passing whims when they spend their time anticipating every wish of yours. But one day you may quarrel over something that matters equally to both of you, and then the people you call weak can be just as stubborn as you.”
“Then we'll fight to the death, won't we, Nelly?” she laughed. “No! I tell you, my faith in Linton's love is so strong that I believe I could kill him and he wouldn't want to strike back.”
I told her his love was all the more reason to value him.

“I do,” she said, “but he needn't whine over trifles. It's childish. Instead of crying because I said Heathcliff now deserved anyone's respect, and that even the finest gentleman in the country would be honoured by his friendship, he ought to have said it himself and shared my delight. He must get used to him and might as well like him. Given the reasons Heathcliff has for disliking him, I'm sure he behaved admirably!”
“What do you think of his staying at Wuthering Heights?” I asked. “He seems completely reformed, a perfect Christian, offering fellowship to every one of his enemies!”

“He explained,” she answered. “It surprises me as much as you. He said he called there for news of me from you, thinking you still lived there. Joseph told Hindley, who came out and questioned him about his activities and how he had been living, then asked him inside. Some people were playing cards. Heathcliff joined them, and my brother lost money to him. Finding he had plenty, Hindley invited him back that evening, and he agreed. Hindley's too reckless to choose his company wisely. He never considers the reasons for distrusting someone he has treated so badly. Heathcliff says his main reason for renewing acquaintance with his old tormentor is to have lodgings within walking distance of the Grange, together with his affection for the house where we lived together. He also hopes I'll have more chances to see him there than if he settled in Gimmerton. He means to offer a generous rent for rooms at the Heights. My brother's greed will doubtless make him accept. He was always greedy, though everything he grasps with one hand he throws away with the other.”
“A fine place for a young man to make his home!” I said. “Aren't you afraid of what may come of it, Mrs. Linton?”

“Not for my friend,” she replied. “His strong head will keep him safe. A little for Hindley, though he can't become any worse morally, and I stand between him and physical harm. Tonight has reconciled me to God and humanity! I had been rebelling angrily against Providence. Oh, Nelly, I've suffered such bitter, bitter misery! If that creature knew how bitter, he'd be ashamed to cloud its passing with pointless petulance. Kindness towards him made me endure it alone. Had I described the agony I often felt, he would have learned to long as intensely as I did for relief. But it's over, and I won't punish his foolishness. After this I can bear anything! If the lowest creature alive slapped my face, I'd not only turn the other cheek but beg its pardon for provoking it. To prove it, I'll make peace with Edgar straight away. Goodnight! I'm an angel!”

With this self-satisfied assurance she left. Next day it was clear she had carried out her resolution successfully. Mr. Linton had not only given up his ill temper, though Catherine's exuberance still seemed to subdue him; he also raised no objection to her taking Isabella to Wuthering Heights that afternoon. She rewarded him with such a summer of sweetness and love that the house became a paradise for several days, master and servants alike enjoying its unbroken sunshine.

At first Heathcliff—Mr. Heathcliff, as I should call him now—used his freedom to visit Thrushcross Grange cautiously, apparently calculating how much intrusion its owner would tolerate. Catherine too thought it wise to restrain her pleasure at receiving him. Gradually he established himself as an expected visitor. He retained much of his childhood reserve, which prevented any startling displays of feeling. My master's uneasiness eased, and new circumstances soon diverted it elsewhere for a time.

The new trouble arose from the unexpected misfortune of Isabella Linton developing a sudden, irresistible attraction to their tolerated guest. She was eighteen then, a charming young woman, childish in her manners despite sharp intelligence, strong feelings and a sharp temper when provoked. Her brother loved her dearly and was appalled at this extraordinary choice. Even apart from the disgrace of marrying a man without family standing, and the possibility of his own property passing into such a man's hands if he left no male heir, Edgar understood Heathcliff's character well enough. He knew that although the outside had changed, the mind within was unaltered and unalterable. That mind frightened and repelled him. He recoiled with foreboding from entrusting Isabella to it. Had he known that her affection was unsolicited and entirely unreturned, he would have shrunk still further; from the moment he discovered it, however, he blamed deliberate scheming by Heathcliff.

For some time we had all noticed Miss Linton worrying and pining over something. She grew irritable and tiresome, constantly snapping at and provoking Catherine, dangerously close to exhausting her limited patience. We partly excused her on grounds of illness, for she was fading and growing thinner before our eyes. But one day she was particularly difficult: she refused breakfast, complained that the servants disobeyed her, that the mistress allowed her no importance in the house, that Edgar neglected her, that open doors had given her a cold and that we deliberately let the parlour fire go out to annoy her, with a hundred even more trivial charges. Mrs. Linton firmly ordered her to bed, scolded her thoroughly and threatened to send for the doctor. At Kenneth's name she immediately declared her health perfect and said only Catherine's cruelty made her unhappy.
“How can you call me cruel, you naughty spoiled thing?” the mistress exclaimed, astonished at so unreasonable a charge. “You must be losing your senses. Tell me when I've been cruel?”
“Yesterday,” Isabella sobbed, “and now!”
“Yesterday!” her sister-in-law repeated. “When was that?”
“When we walked on the moor. You told me to go wherever I wanted while you strolled on with Mr. Heathcliff!”

“You call that cruelty?” Catherine said, laughing. “I wasn’t hinting that your company was unwanted. We didn’t mind whether you stayed with us or not. I simply thought Heathcliff’s conversation wouldn’t interest you.”
“Oh, no,” the young woman wept. “You wanted me gone because you knew I wanted to stay!”
“Is she in her right mind?” Mrs. Linton appealed to me. “Isabella, I'll repeat our whole conversation word for word, and you can tell me what you would have found so charming.”
“I didn't care about the conversation,” she replied. “I wanted to be with—”
“Well?” Catherine prompted, seeing her hesitate before finishing the sentence.
“With him, and I won't always be sent away!” she continued heatedly. “You're a dog in the manger, Cathy. You don't want anyone loved except yourself!”

“You impudent little monkey!” Mrs. Linton exclaimed in astonishment. “But I refuse to believe such stupidity! Surely you can't want Heathcliff's admiration, can't consider him a pleasant man! I hope I've misunderstood you, Isabella?”
“No, you haven't,” the infatuated girl said. “I love him more than you ever loved Edgar, and he might love me if you'd allow him!”

“Then I wouldn't be in your place for a kingdom!” Catherine declared forcefully, and seemed quite sincere. “Nelly, help me show her how mad she is. Tell her what Heathcliff is: an untamed creature, without polish or education, a barren wilderness of gorse and hard rock. I'd as soon turn that little canary loose in the park on a winter day as advise you to give him your heart! Nothing but dreadful ignorance of his character, child, puts such a dream in your head. Please don't imagine depths of kindness and love hidden beneath a severe exterior! He isn't a rough diamond, some rustic oyster with a pearl inside: he's fierce and pitiless, like a wolf. I never tell him, ‘Leave this enemy or that one alone because hurting them would be unkind or cruel.’ I say, ‘Leave them alone because _I_ would hate to see them hurt.’ If he found you a troublesome responsibility, Isabella, he'd crush you like a sparrow's egg. I know he couldn't love a Linton. Yet he'd be quite capable of marrying your money and the inheritance you expect: greed is becoming his ruling sin. There's my portrait of him, and I'm his friend—so much his friend that, if he'd seriously intended to catch you, I might have said nothing and let you walk into the trap.”
Miss Linton stared indignantly at her sister-in-law.
“Shame on you! Shame!” she repeated angrily. “You're worse than twenty enemies, you poisonous friend!”
“Ah! You don't believe me, then?” Catherine asked. “You think I'm speaking out of wicked selfishness?”
“I'm certain of it,” Isabella retorted, “and you make me shudder!”
“Good!” cried the other. “If that's your attitude, find out for yourself. I've finished; your impudent insolence can have the last word.”—

“And I'm the one who must suffer for her selfishness!” Isabella sobbed as Mrs. Linton left. “Everything, everything is against me. She's spoiled my one comfort. But she lied, didn't she? Mr. Heathcliff isn't a devil. His soul is honourable and faithful, or how could he have remembered her?”

“Put him out of your thoughts, Miss,” I told her. “He's a bird of ill omen, no mate for you. Mrs. Linton spoke harshly, but I can't contradict her. She knows his heart better than I do, or anyone else, and would never paint him worse than he is. Honest people don't conceal their actions. How has he been living? Where did his wealth come from? Why stay at Wuthering Heights with a man he hates? They say Mr. Earnshaw has grown worse and worse since his arrival. They're always up all night together; Hindley's borrowing against his land and does nothing but gamble and drink. Only last week I heard this from Joseph when I met him at Gimmerton. ‘Nelly,’ he said, ‘we'll have a coroner's inquest at our place soon. One of 'em's almost had his finger cut off stopping t' other from sticking himself like a calf. That's t' master, ye know, so eager to go before t' great court. He fears no bench o' judges, neither Paul nor Peter nor John nor Matthew, nor any of 'em! He fair longs to set his brazen face against 'em! And that bonny lad Heathcliff, mind ye, he's a rare one. He can grin and laugh at a proper devil's joke as well as anyone. Does he never tell ye of his fine life with us when he visits t' Grange? Here's how it goes: up at sunset, then dice, brandy, shutters closed and candlelight till noon next day. Then t' fool goes cursing and raving to his room, making decent folk stop their ears for shame; and t' knave, why, he counts his money, eats, sleeps and goes off to t' neighbour's to gossip with his wife. Of course he tells Dame Catherine how her father's gold pours into his pocket, and her father's son gallops down t' broad road while he flies ahead to open t' tollgates!’ Now, Miss Linton, Joseph's an old rogue, but no liar. If his account of Heathcliff's behaviour is true, surely you wouldn't want such a husband?”
“You're in league with all the rest, Ellen!” she replied. “I won't hear your slander. How spiteful you must be to want to convince me there's no happiness anywhere!”

I cannot say whether, left alone, she would have outgrown the fancy or cherished it for ever: she had little time for reflection. The following day my master had to attend a meeting of magistrates in the next town. Knowing he would be absent, Mr. Heathcliff called earlier than usual. Catherine and Isabella sat in the library, silent but hostile. Isabella was alarmed by her recent indiscretion and the secret feelings she had revealed in a moment's anger. Catherine, after thinking it over, was truly offended; if she laughed again at her companion's impudence, she meant to make it no laughing matter for _her_. She did laugh when Heathcliff passed the window. I was sweeping the hearth and noticed a mischievous smile on her lips. Isabella, lost in thought or a book, stayed until the door opened, when the chance to escape had passed. She would gladly have taken it if she could.

“Come in, that's right!” the mistress exclaimed cheerfully, drawing a chair to the fire. “Two people here badly need a third to thaw the ice, and you're exactly the person we'd both choose. Heathcliff, at last I can proudly show you someone more devoted to you than I am. You ought to feel flattered. No, not Nelly—don't look at her! My poor little sister-in-law is breaking her heart simply contemplating your bodily and moral beauty. You have it in your power to become Edgar's brother! No, no, Isabella, you mustn't run away,” she continued, catching the bewildered girl, who had risen indignantly, with a show of playfulness. “We were fighting like cats over you, Heathcliff, and she soundly beat me in declarations of devotion and admiration. What's more, she informed me that if I'd have the manners to stand aside, my rival, as she chooses to consider herself, would shoot an arrow into your soul that would hold you for ever and erase my image from your memory for all time!”

“Catherine!” Isabella said, summoning her dignity and refusing to struggle against the firm grip. “Please keep to the truth instead of slandering me, even for fun! Mr. Heathcliff, kindly ask this friend of yours to release me. She forgets that you and I aren't intimate friends, and what amuses her hurts me more than I can say.”
The visitor made no reply, merely sat down and looked entirely indifferent to whatever feelings she had for him. She turned and whispered an earnest plea to her tormentor to let her go.

“Certainly not!” Mrs. Linton replied. “I won't be called a dog in the manger again. You _will_ stay, so there! Heathcliff, why don't you look pleased by my good news? Isabella swears Edgar's love for me is nothing beside hers for you. I'm sure she said something like that, didn't she, Ellen? And she hasn't eaten since our walk two days ago, from grief and rage because I sent her out of your company, supposing you wouldn't welcome it.”
“I think you're misrepresenting her,” Heathcliff said, turning his chair towards them. “At any rate, she wants to leave my company now!”

He stared intently at the girl they were discussing as someone might examine a strange, repulsive animal—a centipede from the Indies, for instance—out of curiosity despite disgust. The poor creature could not endure it. She went pale and red in quick succession; tears gathered on her lashes as she strained her small fingers to loosen Catherine's grip. Every time she lifted one finger from her arm, another pressed down, and she could not remove the whole hand at once. She began using her nails, whose sharp points soon decorated her captor's hand with red crescents.

“What a tigress!” Mrs. Linton exclaimed, releasing her and shaking her hurt hand. “Go, for God's sake, and hide that shrewish face! How foolish to show _him_ your claws. Can't you imagine what he'll conclude? Look, Heathcliff! Those weapons can do damage; you'd better guard your eyes.”

“I'd tear them off her fingers if she ever threatened me,” he answered brutally after she shut the door behind her. “But why were you tormenting the creature like that, Cathy? You weren't telling the truth, were you?”

“I assure you I was,” she answered. “She's been wasting away over you for weeks. This morning she raved about you and poured abuse on me because I described your faults plainly to cool her worship. But don't pursue it. I only wanted to punish her cheek. I like her too much, my dear Heathcliff, to let you actually catch her and devour her.”

“And I like her too little to try,” he said, “except in a very ghoulish sense. You'd hear strange stories if I lived alone with that sickly, waxen face. The most ordinary would be my painting all the rainbow's colours over its white and turning those blue eyes black every day or two: they're disgustingly like Linton's.”
“Delightfully like!” Catherine remarked. “They're dove's eyes—an angel's!”
“She's her brother's heir, isn't she?” he asked after a short silence.

“I'd be sorry to think so,” his companion replied. “Half a dozen nephews will cancel her claim, Heaven willing! Put it out of your mind for now. You're too inclined to covet your neighbour's goods; remember _this_ neighbour's goods belong to me.”
“If they belonged to _me_, they'd be no less yours,” Heathcliff said. “But though Isabella Linton may be foolish, she's hardly mad. In any case, let's drop the subject as you suggest.”

They stopped speaking of it, and Catherine probably stopped thinking of it. The other, I was certain, returned to it often that evening. Whenever Mrs. Linton had to leave the room, I saw him smile to himself—or rather grin—and sink into ominous reflection.

I resolved to watch what he did. My sympathies invariably lay with the master rather than Catherine, and I thought with good reason: he was kind, trusting and honourable. She could not be called the _opposite_, yet she gave herself so much freedom that I had little faith in her principles and even less sympathy with her feelings. I hoped something would quietly rid both Wuthering Heights and the Grange of Mr. Heathcliff, restoring us to our life before he came. His visits were a constant nightmare for me and, I suspected, for my master. His presence at the Heights weighed on me beyond words. I felt God had abandoned the wandering sheep there to its wicked straying, while an evil beast prowled between it and the fold, waiting for its moment to spring and destroy.

chapters.title: Chapter XI
paragraphs: Sometimes, thinking over these matters alone, I rose in sudden terror and put on my bonnet to go and see how things stood at the farm. I persuaded my conscience that I ought to warn him what people were saying about his behaviour. Then I remembered how firmly his bad habits held him, and, despairing of doing him any good, shrank from entering that gloomy house again, unsure I could bear the fulfilment of my own warnings.

Once, on my way to Gimmerton, I made a detour past the old gate. It was about the time my story has now reached, a bright, frosty afternoon, with bare ground and a dry, hard road. I came to the stone where the road branches left onto the moor: a rough sandstone pillar with W. H. cut into its northern side, G. on the east and T. G. on the southwest, pointing to the Heights, the village and the Grange. Yellow sunlight on its grey top reminded me of summer, and I cannot explain why, but suddenly my heart flooded with the feelings of childhood. Hindley and I had loved that spot twenty years earlier. I stared for a long time at the weathered stone, then bent down and saw a hole near its base still full of snail shells and pebbles, which we used to store there with things that did not last so well. As vividly as in real life, I seemed to see my childhood playmate on the withered grass, his dark, square head bent, his small hand scraping earth out with a piece of slate. “Poor Hindley!” I exclaimed without meaning to. I started: for a moment my actual eyes were deceived into seeing the child lift his face and look straight into mine! He vanished instantly, but I felt an irresistible longing to reach the Heights. Superstition urged me to follow it: suppose he was dead! I thought—or soon to die! Suppose this was a death warning! The nearer I came, the more agitated I grew; when the house appeared I shook in every limb. The apparition had got there first and stood peering through the gate. That was my first thought on seeing a brown-eyed boy with tangled hair press his rosy face against the bars. A moment's reflection told me it must be Hareton, _my_ Hareton, little changed from the child I had left ten months before.
“God bless thee, darling!” I cried, forgetting my foolish fears at once. “Hareton, it's Nelly! Thy nurse, Nelly.”
He moved beyond my reach and picked up a big flint.
“I've come to see thy father, Hareton,” I added, guessing from this action that, if he remembered Nelly at all, he did not recognise her in me.

He lifted the stone to throw it. I began speaking soothingly but could not stop his hand: it struck my bonnet. Then a string of curses came stumbling from the little boy's lips, delivered with practised force whether or not he understood them, twisting his baby face into a shocking look of malice. You may be sure I felt more hurt than angry. Almost crying, I took an orange from my pocket and offered it to win him over. After hesitating he snatched it from me, as though he thought I only meant to tempt him and refuse it. I produced another, holding it beyond his reach.
“Who taught you such fine language, my little bairn?” I asked. “Was it the curate?”
“Damn t' curate and thee! Give me that,” he answered.
“Tell me where you learned it and you can have it,” I said. “Who's teaching you?”
“Devil daddy,” he answered.
“And what lessons does daddy give you?” I went on.
He jumped for the orange and I lifted it higher. “What does he teach you?” I repeated.
“Nowt,” he said, “except to keep out of his way. Daddy can't stand me because I swear at him.”
“Ah! And the devil teaches you to swear at your father?” I remarked.
“Aye—no,” he said slowly.
“Then who does?”
“Heathcliff.”
I asked whether he was fond of Mr. Heathcliff.
“Aye!” he replied again.
When I tried to discover why, all I could get was, “I don't know. He pays dad back for what he gives me—he swears at daddy for swearing at me. Says I must do as I like.”
“So the curate isn't giving you lessons in reading and writing?” I asked next.
“No. They said t' curate would have his —— teeth knocked down his —— throat if he crossed t' doorstep. Heathcliff promised that!”

I gave him the orange and told him to inform his father that a woman named Nelly Dean was waiting by the garden gate to speak to him. He went up the path and inside, but Heathcliff, not Hindley, appeared on the doorstep. I immediately turned and ran down the road as fast as I could, not stopping until I reached the signpost, frightened as though I had summoned a goblin. This has little to do with Miss Isabella's affair, except that it strengthened my resolve to keep a close watch and do everything possible to prevent such corruption spreading to the Grange, even if thwarting Mrs. Linton's pleasure brought on a household storm.

When Heathcliff next visited, my young lady happened to be feeding pigeons in the courtyard. For three days she had not spoken to her sister-in-law, but she had also stopped her fretful complaints, which was a great relief. I knew Heathcliff never wasted an unnecessary courtesy on Miss Linton. Now, as soon as he saw her, he first carefully surveyed the entire front of the house. I stood at the kitchen window but stepped out of sight. He crossed the paving stones and spoke to her. She looked embarrassed and anxious to leave, so he put a hand on her arm to stop her. She turned her face away; apparently he asked something she did not want to answer. After another quick glance at the house, believing himself unseen, the scoundrel had the audacity to embrace her.
“Judas! Traitor!” I burst out. “So you're a hypocrite as well? A deliberate cheat.”
“Who is, Nelly?” Catherine asked beside me. I had watched the pair outside too intently to notice her arrival.

“That worthless friend of yours!” I replied hotly. “That sneaking rogue out there. Ah, he's seen us—he's coming inside! I wonder if he'll dare find a plausible excuse for courting Miss after telling you he hated her?”

Mrs. Linton saw Isabella break free and run into the garden. A minute later Heathcliff opened the door. I could not help giving vent to some of my outrage, but Catherine angrily ordered me to be quiet, threatening to send me out of the kitchen if I dared presume to put in my insolent opinions.

“Anyone hearing you would think you were the mistress!” she cried. “You need putting in your proper place! Heathcliff, what do you mean by causing this disturbance? I told you to leave Isabella alone! Please do, unless you're tired of being welcomed here and want Linton to lock you out!”
“God help him if he tries!” answered the dark villain—I hated him at that moment. “God keep him gentle and patient! Every day I'm more desperate to send him to heaven!”
“Hush!” Catherine said, closing the inner door. “Don't upset me. Why did you ignore my request? Did she deliberately put herself in your way?”
“What's that to you?” he growled. “I've a right to kiss her if she wants me to, and you've no right to complain. I'm not _your_ husband; _you_ have no reason to be jealous of me!”

“I'm not jealous of you,” the mistress replied. “I'm jealous on your behalf. Stop looking like that: you won't scowl at me! If you love Isabella, you shall marry her. But do you love her? Tell me honestly, Heathcliff! There, you won't answer. I'm sure you don't.”
“Would Mr. Linton agree to his sister marrying such a man?” I asked.
“Mr. Linton would have to agree,” my mistress answered firmly.

“He could save himself the trouble,” Heathcliff said. “I'd manage perfectly well without his approval. As for you, Catherine, while we're on the subject there's something I want to say. Understand that I _know_ you've treated me hellishly—hellishly! Do you hear? If you flatter yourself that I haven't noticed, you're a fool. If you think sweet words can console me, you're an idiot; and if you imagine I'll suffer without revenge, I'll soon show you otherwise! Meanwhile, thank you for revealing your sister-in-law's secret. I swear I'll make the most of it. And you keep out of the way!”

“What new side to his character is this?” Mrs. Linton exclaimed in amazement. “I've treated you hellishly, and you'll have revenge! How will you take it, you ungrateful brute? What have I done to you that's hellish?”

“I don't want revenge on you,” Heathcliff answered more quietly. “That isn't my plan. A tyrant grinds down his slaves, and instead of attacking him, they crush the people beneath them. You're welcome to torture me to death for your amusement: just let me amuse myself a little in the same way, and avoid insulting me as much as you can. After demolishing my palace, don't put up a hut and congratulate yourself on your kindness in giving me a home. If I believed you truly wanted me to marry Isabel, I'd cut my throat!”

“Oh, the trouble is that I'm _not_ jealous, is it?” Catherine exclaimed. “Well, I won't offer you a wife again. It's like offering Satan a lost soul: your happiness, like his, lies in causing misery, and you're proving it. Edgar has recovered from the bad temper your arrival put him in; I'm beginning to feel safe and peaceful. You can't bear to know we're at peace, and seem determined to stir up a quarrel. Quarrel with Edgar if you like, Heathcliff, and deceive his sister: that will be exactly the most effective revenge you can take on me.”

The conversation stopped. Mrs. Linton sat down beside the fire, flushed and gloomy. The spirit she had enlisted was becoming unmanageable: she could neither dismiss nor control it. He stood on the hearth, arms folded, brooding over his evil thoughts. I left them like this to find the master, who was wondering why Catherine remained downstairs so long.
“Ellen,” he asked when I came in, “have you seen where your mistress is?”

“Yes, sir, she's in the kitchen,” I replied. “Mr. Heathcliff's behaviour has upset her terribly. I really think the conditions of his visits need changing. Being too lenient does harm, and now matters have reached this point—” I described the scene outside and, as fully as I dared, the argument afterwards. I thought it could do Mrs. Linton little damage unless she chose to make it worse by defending her guest. Edgar Linton could hardly wait for me to finish. His first words showed that he did not consider his wife blameless.

“This is unbearable!” he exclaimed. “It's disgraceful that she calls him a friend and forces his company on me! Fetch two men from the hall, Ellen. Catherine won't stay down there arguing with that low ruffian any longer. I've indulged her quite enough.”

He went downstairs, told the servants to wait in the passage, and entered the kitchen with me behind him. The occupants had resumed their angry discussion; at least Mrs. Linton was scolding with fresh energy. Heathcliff had gone to the window and stood with his head lowered, apparently somewhat subdued by her fierce rebukes. He saw the master first and quickly signalled her to stop. Once she saw why, she fell abruptly silent.

“What is the meaning of this?” Linton asked her. “What sense of decency can you have, staying here after the way that scoundrel has spoken to you? I suppose it means nothing to you because that's how he always speaks. You're accustomed to his vileness, and perhaps expect me to become accustomed to it too!”

“Have you been eavesdropping, Edgar?” the mistress asked, in a voice peculiarly suited to provoking her husband, suggesting both indifference and contempt for his anger. Heathcliff had looked up during Edgar's speech; at Catherine's question he laughed scornfully, apparently intending to draw Mr. Linton's attention. He succeeded, but Edgar had no intention of entertaining him with extravagant anger.

“Until now, sir, I've treated you with patience,” he said quietly. “Not because I failed to understand your miserable, degraded character, but because I thought you only partly responsible for it. Catherine wished to maintain your acquaintance, and I foolishly agreed. Your presence is a moral poison that could corrupt the most virtuous person. For that reason, and to avoid worse consequences, I forbid you to enter this house again and now require you to leave immediately. If you delay three minutes, your departure will be forced and disgraceful.”
With a contemptuous eye, Heathcliff measured both the speaker's height and his breadth.
“Cathy, your lamb is making threats like a bull!” he said. “It risks cracking its skull against my fists. By God! Mr. Linton, I'm terribly sorry you aren't worth knocking down!”

My master glanced towards the passage and signalled for me to summon the men; he meant to risk no personal fight. I obeyed, but Mrs. Linton, suspecting something, followed me. As I tried to call them, she pulled me back, slammed the door and locked it.

“Fair play!” she said in answer to her husband's angry, astonished look. “If you aren't brave enough to attack him yourself, apologise or submit to a beating. That'll cure you of pretending to more courage than you have. No, I'll swallow the key before I give it up! What a lovely reward for my kindness to both of you! After endlessly indulging one man's weakness and the other's bad nature, my thanks are two examples of blind ingratitude, ridiculously stupid! Edgar, I was defending you and your family, and I hope Heathcliff beats you sick for daring to think ill of me!”

The master needed no beating to make him sick. He tried to wrest the key from Catherine's hand, and she threw it into the hottest part of the fire for safety. Mr. Edgar began trembling nervously and turned deathly pale. Nothing he could do prevented that overwhelming emotion: anguish and humiliation together defeated him completely. He leaned against the back of a chair and covered his face.

“Oh, heavens! In former days this would have earned you a knighthood!” Mrs. Linton exclaimed. “We're defeated! We're defeated! Heathcliff is no more likely to raise a finger against you than the king to send his army against a colony of mice. Cheer up! You won't be hurt! You're not a lamb, you're a little hare still at its mother's milk.”

“I wish you happiness with your milk-blooded coward, Cathy!” her friend said. “My compliments on your taste. And this drooling, trembling thing is what you preferred to me! I wouldn't strike him with my fist, but I'd kick him with my foot and enjoy it considerably. Is he crying, or about to faint from fright?”

The fellow stepped closer and shoved the chair Linton leaned on. He would have done better to keep his distance: my master sprang upright and struck him squarely in the throat, a blow that would have felled a less strongly built man. It left him breathless for a minute. While he choked, Mr. Linton walked through the back door into the yard and round to the front entrance.

“There! That's the end of your visits,” Catherine cried. “Go now: he'll be back with two pistols and half a dozen men. If he heard what we said, of course he'll never forgive you. You've done me an ill turn, Heathcliff! But leave—hurry! I'd rather see Edgar cornered than you.”

“Do you think I'm leaving with that blow burning in my throat?” he thundered. “By hell, no! I'll crush his ribs like a rotten hazelnut before I cross that threshold! If I don't knock him down now, I'll murder him some day. So if you value his life, let me get at him!”

“He isn't coming,” I interrupted, inventing a small lie. “It's the coachman and both gardeners. Surely you won't wait for them to throw you into the road! They've each got a club, and the master will probably watch from the parlour windows to make sure they obey.”

The coachman and gardeners _were_ there, but Linton was with them. They had already entered the yard. On reflection, Heathcliff decided to avoid fighting three servants. He seized the poker, smashed the lock off the inner door and escaped as they came stamping in.
Mrs. Linton, in great agitation, told me to come upstairs with her. She did not know how much I had contributed to the disturbance, and I wanted to keep her ignorant.

“I'm almost out of my mind, Nelly!” she exclaimed, throwing herself onto the sofa. “A thousand blacksmiths' hammers are pounding in my head! Tell Isabella to keep away. All this is her fault, and if she or anyone else provokes me now, I'll go wild. And Nelly, if you see Edgar again tonight, tell him I'm in danger of serious illness. I hope it proves true. He's shocked and distressed me dreadfully! I want to frighten him. Besides, he might come here and begin abusing me or complaining. I'm sure I'd accuse him in return, and God knows where we'd finish! Will you tell him, my good Nelly? You know I'm not to blame for any of this. What possessed him to listen? Heathcliff spoke outrageously after you left, but I could soon have turned him away from Isabella, and the rest meant nothing. Now everything's ruined by that foolish craving some people have, like a demon haunting them, to hear themselves spoken ill of! If Edgar had never overheard, the conversation would have done him no harm. Really, when he started on me in that unreasonably angry tone, after I'd scolded Heathcliff hoarse for _his_ sake, I scarcely cared what they did to each other. Especially since I felt that, whatever happened, we'd all be driven apart for who knows how long! Well, if I can't keep Heathcliff as my friend, if Edgar insists on being mean and jealous, I'll try to break their hearts by breaking mine. When they drive me to extremes, that would end everything quickly! But it's a last desperate measure; I wouldn't spring it on Linton without warning. Until now he's sensibly feared provoking me. You must explain the danger of changing that policy and remind him how close my passionate temper comes to frenzy once it's roused. I wish you'd get rid of that indifferent look and show a little more concern for me.”

My unmoved reception of these instructions was doubtless infuriating, for she spoke in complete sincerity. But I thought that someone able to plan beforehand how to profit from fits of passion could, by using her will, control herself fairly well even while they lasted. I had no wish to “frighten” her husband, as she put it, and increase his troubles to serve her selfish purposes. So when I met the master heading towards the parlour, I said nothing. I did take the liberty of turning back to hear whether they would quarrel again. He spoke first.

“Stay where you are, Catherine,” he said, without anger but in a deeply sorrowful, dejected voice. “I won't stay. I've come neither to argue nor to make peace. I only want to know whether, after tonight, you mean to continue your close friendship with—”

“Oh, for pity's sake,” the mistress interrupted, stamping her foot, “for pity's sake, say no more about it now! Your cold blood can never rise to a fever; your veins are full of icy water, but mine are boiling, and seeing your coldness makes them leap.”

“Answer my question and I'll go,” Mr. Linton persisted. “You _must_ answer, and this violence doesn't frighten me. I've discovered you can be as self-controlled as anyone when you choose. Will you give up Heathcliff, or give up me? You can't be _my_ friend and _his_ together, and I absolutely _insist_ on knowing which you choose.”
“I insist on being left alone!” Catherine exclaimed furiously. “I demand it! Can't you see I can barely stand? Edgar, you—you must leave me!”

She rang the bell until it broke with a twang; I came in slowly. Such senseless, wicked rages would try a saint's patience! She lay banging her head against the sofa's arm and grinding her teeth as though she meant to shatter them! Mr. Linton stood watching, suddenly full of remorse and fear, and told me to bring water. She had no breath to speak. I fetched a full glass, and when she refused to drink I sprinkled her face. Within seconds she stretched out rigidly and rolled her eyes upward; her cheeks, at once pale and discoloured, took on the appearance of death. Linton looked terrified.
“There's absolutely nothing wrong with her,” I whispered. I didn't want him to give in, though inwardly I could not help feeling afraid.
“Her lips are bloody!” he said with a shudder.

“Never mind!” I answered sharply, and told him that before he came she had planned to display a fit of madness. Carelessly I said this aloud, and she heard. She sprang up, hair flying over her shoulders, eyes flashing, the muscles of her neck and arms standing out unnaturally. I expected broken bones at the very least. Instead she glared round for an instant and rushed away. The master told me to follow, and I did, as far as her bedroom door, which she locked against me.

When she made no move to come down for breakfast next morning, I went to ask if she wanted it brought up. “No!” she replied firmly. I asked again at dinner and tea, and again the following day, always receiving the same answer. Mr. Linton spent his time in the library without asking what his wife was doing. He and Isabella had talked for an hour while he tried to draw from her a properly horrified response to Heathcliff's advances. Her evasive answers told him nothing, and he had to end the questioning unsatisfied. He did, however, solemnly warn her that if she were mad enough to encourage that worthless suitor, every family tie between them would be broken.

chapters.title: Chapter XII
paragraphs: While Miss Linton wandered miserably through the park and garden, always silent and nearly always crying, her brother shut himself away with books he never opened. I imagined he was wearing himself out waiting for Catherine to regret her behaviour, come of her own accord to ask forgiveness, and make peace. Meanwhile, _she_ stubbornly refused to eat, probably imagining that at every meal Edgar was almost choking over her absence, and that only pride stopped him from rushing to throw himself at her feet. I went about my work convinced that there was only one sensible person inside the Grange, and that person was me. I wasted no sympathy on Miss Isabella, no arguments on my mistress, and very little attention on my master's sighs. Since he could not hear his wife's voice, he longed at least to hear her name. As far as I was concerned, they could sort themselves out however they liked. It was a tiresomely slow business, but eventually I began to welcome what seemed to be the first faint sign of progress—or so I thought at first.

On the third day Mrs. Linton unbolted her door. She had emptied both her water jug and her decanter, and asked for more water and a bowl of gruel, saying she believed she was dying. I took this to be a speech intended for Edgar. I believed nothing of the sort, so I kept it to myself and brought her tea and dry toast. She ate and drank eagerly, then fell back against her pillow, clenching her hands and groaning. “Oh, I will die,” she cried, “since nobody cares anything about me. I wish I hadn't eaten that.” Much later I heard her mutter, “No, I won't die—he'd be pleased—he doesn't love me at all—he would never miss me!”
“Did you need anything, ma'am?” I asked. I still kept an outward appearance of calm, despite her deathly face and her strange, overblown behaviour.
“What is that unfeeling creature doing?” she demanded, pushing the thick tangles of hair away from her shrunken face. “Has he sunk into a stupor, or is he dead?”
“Neither, if you mean Mr. Linton,” I answered. “I think he's fairly well, although he spends rather too much time studying. He's always with his books, as he has no other company.”
Had I understood how ill she really was, I would never have said that. But I could not shake off my belief that some of her illness was an act.

“With his books!” she cried in disbelief. “And I'm dying! I'm at the edge of the grave! My God! Does he know how I've changed?” She stared at herself in the mirror on the opposite wall. “Is that Catherine Linton? He thinks I'm sulking—perhaps only playing. Can't you tell him this is terribly serious? Nelly, if it isn't too late, once I know how he feels I'll choose between two things: either starve myself straight away—which would be no punishment to him unless he had a heart—or recover and leave the country. Are you telling me the truth about him? Be careful. Does he really care so little whether I live?”
“Why, ma'am,” I said, “the master has no idea that your mind is disturbed. Naturally he doesn't fear that you'll let yourself die of hunger.”
“You don't think so? Can't you tell him I will?” she replied. “Make him believe it! Tell him it's your own opinion: say you're certain I will!”
“No, Mrs. Linton, you're forgetting,” I pointed out, “that you ate quite heartily this evening. Tomorrow you'll feel the benefit of it.”

“If only I knew it would kill him,” she broke in, “I'd kill myself this instant! Through these three dreadful nights I haven't closed my eyes—and oh, how I've suffered! I've been haunted, Nelly! But I'm beginning to think you don't like me. How strange! I thought that even if everyone hated and despised one another, they couldn't help loving me. And in a few hours they've all become my enemies. _They_ have, I'm sure of it—the people _here_. How miserable to die with all their cold faces round me! Isabella, frightened and disgusted, not daring to enter the room because watching Catherine die would be so dreadful. And Edgar standing solemnly by, waiting for it to end; then thanking God for bringing peace back to his house, and going back to his _books_! In the name of everything that has a feeling heart, what business has he with _books_ while I'm dying?”

She could not endure the picture I had planted in her mind of Mr. Linton calmly accepting her fate. She tossed about until her feverish confusion became frenzy, and tore her pillow with her teeth. Then she sat up, burning hot, and asked me to open the window. It was the middle of winter, with a strong wind from the northeast, and I refused. The expressions passing across her face and her sudden changes of mood now frightened me badly. I remembered her earlier illness and the doctor's warning that we must not oppose her. A moment before she had been violent; now she propped herself on one arm and seemed quite unaware of my refusal. Like a child playing, she pulled feathers through the holes she had torn and arranged them on the sheet according to the birds they came from. Her thoughts had wandered elsewhere.

“That's from a turkey,” she murmured to herself, “and this is a wild duck's, and this a pigeon's. Ah, they've put pigeon's feathers in the pillows—no wonder I couldn't die! I must remember to throw it on the floor when I lie down. And here's a moor-cock's; and this one—I'd know it among a thousand—it's a lapwing's. A bonny bird, circling above our heads out in the middle of the moor. It wanted to reach its nest: the clouds had come down on the hills and it could feel rain coming. We picked this feather up from the heather; nobody shot the bird. In winter we found its nest full of little skeletons. Heathcliff had set a trap over it, and the parents dared not come back. Afterwards I made him promise never to shoot a lapwing, and he never did. Yes, here are more! Did he shoot my lapwings, Nelly? Are any of them red? Let me see.”

“Stop that childish nonsense!” I interrupted, pulling the pillow away and turning the holes towards the mattress, for she was emptying it by the handful. “Lie down and close your eyes. Your mind is wandering. What a mess! The down's blowing about like snow.”
I moved around the room gathering it up.

“When I look at you, Nelly,” she continued dreamily, “I see an old woman, with grey hair and bent shoulders. This bed is the fairy cave beneath Penistone Crags, and you're collecting elf-bolts to harm our heifers. While I'm here you pretend they're only scraps of wool. That's what you'll be in fifty years: I know you're not like that now. My mind isn't wandering; you're wrong. Otherwise I'd believe you really _were_ that shrivelled witch, and that I _was_ under Penistone Crags. But I know it's night, and there are two candles on the table, making the black cupboard shine like jet.”
“The black cupboard? Where?” I asked. “You're talking in your sleep!”
“Against the wall, where it always is,” she answered. “It _does_ look strange—there's a face in it!”
“There isn't a cupboard in this room, and there never has been,” I said. I sat down again, fastening back the curtain so I could watch her.
“Can't _you_ see that face?” she asked, staring hard into the mirror.
Nothing I said could make her understand that it was her own face. At last I got up and covered the mirror with a shawl.
“It's still behind there!” she went on anxiously. “And it moved. Who is it? I hope it won't come out when you've gone! Oh! Nelly, this room is haunted! I'm afraid to be left alone!”
I held her hand and told her to be calm. One shudder after another shook her whole body, and she kept insisting on staring towards the mirror.
“There's nobody here!” I told her firmly. “It was _you_, Mrs. Linton. A little while ago you knew that.”
“Me!” she gasped. “And the clock's striking twelve! Then it's true! How dreadful!”
She gripped the bedclothes and pulled them over her eyes. I tried to slip to the door to call her husband, but a piercing scream brought me back: the shawl had fallen off the mirror.
“Why, what _is_ wrong?” I cried. “Who's the coward now? Wake up! That's the looking-glass—the mirror, Mrs. Linton. You're seeing yourself, and there I am beside you.”
She clung to me, trembling and confused. Gradually, though, the terror left her face, and a flush of shame replaced its deathly pallor.

“Oh, dear! I thought I was at home,” she sighed. “I thought I was lying in my own room at Wuthering Heights. I'm so weak that my head got muddled, and I screamed without knowing what I was doing. Don't say anything; just stay with me. I'm afraid to sleep. My dreams terrify me.”
“A good sleep would help you, ma'am,” I replied. “And I hope all this suffering will stop you from trying to starve yourself again.”

“Oh, if only I were in my own bed in the old house!” she went on bitterly, wringing her hands. “With the wind sounding through the fir trees outside the window. Let me feel it—it blows straight down from the moor—please let me have one breath!”

To soothe her, I opened the casement a little for a few seconds. An icy gust swept in; I shut it and went back to her side. Now she lay still, her face streaming with tears. Physical exhaustion had completely broken her spirit. Our fiery Catherine had become no stronger than a crying child.
“How long have I been shut in here?” she asked, suddenly rousing herself.
“You shut yourself in on Monday evening,” I answered, “and now it's Thursday night—or rather, Friday morning.”
“What! In the same week?” she cried. “Has it only been that little time?”
“Long enough to live on nothing but cold water and bad temper,” I remarked.

“Well, it seems such a weary stretch of hours,” she muttered uncertainly. “It must be longer. I remember being in the parlour after their quarrel, and Edgar provoking me cruelly, and rushing into this room in despair. The moment I bolted the door everything went black, and I fell to the floor. I couldn't explain to Edgar how certain I was that I'd have a fit, or go raving mad, if he kept tormenting me! I couldn't control my tongue or my thoughts. Perhaps he didn't understand my agony: I barely had enough sense left to try to escape him and his voice. By the time I could see and hear properly again, dawn was breaking. Nelly, I'll tell you what I thought then, and what has come back again and again until I've feared for my sanity. As I lay with my head against that table leg, barely able to make out the grey square of the window, I thought I was inside the oak-panelled bed at home. My heart ached with some terrible grief which I couldn't remember just after waking. I lay thinking and tormenting myself, trying to discover what it was; and, strangest of all, the last seven years of my life had vanished! I couldn't remember their ever happening. I was a child; my father had just been buried, and I was miserable because Hindley had ordered Heathcliff and me to be separated. For the first time I had been put to sleep alone. After a night of crying I woke from a wretched doze and raised my hand to slide back the panels. It hit the tabletop! I swept it across the carpet, and then my memory came flooding back. My first grief disappeared beneath a convulsion of despair. I can't explain why I felt so desperately miserable. I must have been out of my mind for a moment, because there's hardly any reason for it. But imagine that, at twelve years old, I had been torn away from the Heights, from everything I'd known as a child, and from the person who was everything to me—as Heathcliff was then—and changed in a single instant into Mrs. Linton, mistress of Thrushcross Grange and wife to a stranger. From then on, an exile and an outcast from everything that had been my world. That may give you some idea of the pit I was crawling in! Shake your head all you like, Nelly: _you've_ helped to drive me out of my senses! You should have spoken to Edgar—you really should—and made him leave me in peace! Oh, I'm burning! I wish I were outside! I wish I were a girl again, half wild and tough and free, laughing at injuries instead of going mad over them! Why have I changed so much? Why do a few words send my blood into such hellish turmoil? I'm sure I'd be myself again if I could get among the heather on those hills. Open the window again, wide, and fasten it back! Hurry—why don't you move?”
“Because I won't let you catch your death of cold,” I answered.
“You mean you won't give me a chance to live,” she said sullenly. “Well, I'm not helpless yet. I'll open it myself.”

Before I could stop her she slid out of bed, staggered across the room, flung the window open, and leaned out. She took no notice of the freezing air cutting round her shoulders like a knife. I begged her to come away and finally tried to pull her back. But I soon found that the strength of her delirium was far greater than mine. Her later words and actions convinced me that she _was_ delirious. There was no moon; below us everything lay in a dark mist. Not a light shone from a house, near or far: they had all been put out long before. The lights of Wuthering Heights could never be seen from there in any case, yet she insisted she could see them shining.

“Look!” she cried eagerly. “That's my room, with the candle burning and the trees waving in front of it. The other candle's in Joseph's attic. Joseph stays up late, doesn't he? He's waiting for me to come home so he can lock the gate. Well, he'll have to wait a while longer. It's a hard journey, with a sad heart to make it, and we must go past Gimmerton church along the way! We've often faced its ghosts together, daring each other to stand among the graves and call them out. But, Heathcliff, if I dare you now, will you come? If you do, I'll keep you. I won't lie there alone. They can bury me twelve feet deep and bring the church down on top of me, but I won't rest until you're with me. I never will!”

She stopped, then went on with a strange smile. “He's thinking it over—he'd rather I came to him! Find a way, then! Not through that churchyard. How slow you are! Be satisfied; you've always followed me!”

I saw that arguing with her madness was useless. I was trying to work out how to reach something to wrap round her without letting go of her—for I dared not leave her alone at that wide-open window—when, to my dismay, the door handle rattled and Mr. Linton came in. He had only just left the library. As he passed along the hall, he had heard our voices and been drawn by curiosity, or fear, to find out what we were doing up at such an hour.

“Oh, sir!” I cried, cutting short the exclamation that rose to his lips at the sight before him and the bitter cold of the room. “My poor mistress is ill, and she's too much for me. I can't manage her at all. Please come and persuade her to go to bed. Put your anger aside: it's hard to guide her any way except the one she chooses.”
“Catherine ill?” he said, hurrying towards us. “Close the window, Ellen! Catherine! Why—”
He stopped. The sight of Mrs. Linton's wasted face struck him speechless. He could only look from her to me in horrified astonishment.

“She has been upsetting herself in here,” I continued, “and hardly eating, without making any complaint. She wouldn't let any of us in until this evening, so we couldn't tell you how she was, because we didn't know ourselves. But it's nothing.”

I knew my explanations sounded clumsy. The master frowned. “Nothing, is it, Ellen Dean?” he said sternly. “You'll give me a better explanation for keeping me in ignorance of this!” He took his wife in his arms and gazed at her in anguish.

At first she showed no sign of knowing him. Her distracted eyes seemed unable to see him at all. But the delirium did not hold her continuously. Once her eyes had been drawn away from the darkness outside, her attention slowly settled on him, and she realised who was holding her.

“Ah! So you've come, Edgar Linton?” she said, suddenly fierce. “You're one of those creatures who always turn up when they're least wanted, and never when they are! I suppose we'll have plenty of weeping now—I can see we will—but that won't keep me from my narrow home out there, my resting place, where I'll be before spring is over! There it is: not with the Lintons under the chapel roof, mind you, but outside in the open air, with a headstone. You can choose for yourself whether to go to them or come to me!”
“Catherine, what have you done?” the master began. “Do I mean nothing to you any more? Do you love that wretch Heath—”

“Be quiet!” cried Mrs. Linton. “Quiet, this instant! Say that name and I'll settle everything by jumping from the window! You can have what you're touching now, but before you touch me again my soul will be on that hilltop. I don't want you, Edgar. I'm beyond wanting you. Go back to your books. I'm glad you have something to comfort you, because everything you had in me is gone.”
“Her mind is wandering, sir,” I put in. “She's been talking nonsense all evening. Give her peace and proper care, and she'll recover. From now on we must be careful how we upset her.”

“I want no more advice from you,” Mr. Linton answered. “You knew what your mistress was like, and you encouraged me to torment her. And you gave me no hint of her condition in all these three days! It was heartless! Months of illness couldn't have changed her this much!”

I started to defend myself. It seemed too much to be blamed for someone else's wicked wilfulness. “I knew Mrs. Linton was stubborn and domineering,” I cried, “but I didn't know you wanted me to encourage her violent temper! I didn't know I was meant to turn a blind eye to Mr. Heathcliff just to humour her. I did my duty as a loyal servant by telling you, and now I've had a loyal servant's reward! Well, I'll know to be more careful next time. Next time you can find things out for yourself!”
“The next time you bring me tales, Ellen Dean, you will leave my service,” he replied.

“So you would rather hear nothing about it, Mr. Linton?” I said. “Heathcliff has your permission to court Miss Isabella, and to drop in whenever you're away, for the express purpose of turning my mistress against you?”
Confused though Catherine was, she quickly understood how our conversation concerned her.

“Ah! Nelly has betrayed me,” she cried furiously. “Nelly is my secret enemy. You witch! So you really are gathering elf-bolts to hurt us! Let me go, and I'll make her regret it! I'll make her scream that she takes it back!”

Mad fury blazed in her eyes. She fought desperately to free herself from Linton's arms. I had no wish to stay and see what happened. Deciding to take responsibility myself for getting medical help, I left the room.

As I crossed the garden towards the road, I noticed something white moving near a bridle hook fixed into the wall. Its jerky movements were plainly caused by something other than the wind. Despite my hurry, I stopped to examine it: otherwise I knew my imagination might forever insist I had seen something from the other world. To my great surprise and bewilderment, I discovered, more by touch than sight, that Miss Isabella's spaniel, Fanny, was hanging by a handkerchief and almost at its last breath. I quickly freed the animal and lifted it into the garden. I had seen it follow its mistress upstairs when she went to bed, and could not imagine how it had got outside or who had been cruel enough to do this. While I was undoing the knot round the hook, I thought I repeatedly heard horses galloping some distance away. But there was so much else on my mind that I barely thought about it, strange as the sound was in that place at two in the morning.

Fortunately, as I came up the village street, Mr. Kenneth was just leaving his house to visit a patient. My account of Catherine Linton's illness persuaded him to return with me at once. He was a blunt, rough man, and did not hesitate to say he doubted she would survive this second attack unless she followed his instructions more willingly than she had before.

“Nelly Dean,” he said, “I can't help thinking there's something more behind this. What's been happening at the Grange? We've heard some strange reports up here. A strong, healthy lass like Catherine doesn't fall ill over nothing—and people of that sort shouldn't, either. Getting them through a fever and suchlike is hard work. How did it start?”

“The master will tell you,” I answered. “But you know what violent tempers the Earnshaws have, and Mrs. Linton is worse than any of them. I can tell you this much: it began with a quarrel. In the middle of a furious rage she had some kind of fit. At least that's what she says, because she rushed off at the height of it and locked herself away. Afterwards she wouldn't eat, and now she goes from raving to a sort of half-dream. She knows the people round her, but her head is full of strange ideas and things she imagines.”
“Mr. Linton will be upset?” Kenneth asked.
“Upset? If anything happens to her, his heart will break!” I answered. “Don't frighten him any more than you must.”
“Well, I warned him to be careful,” my companion said. “He'll have to bear the consequences of ignoring me! Hasn't he been on friendly terms with Mr. Heathcliff lately?”

“Heathcliff often visits the Grange,” I replied, “though that's more because my mistress knew him as a boy than because the master enjoys his company. Just now he has been relieved of the trouble of calling, after showing some presumptuous intentions towards Miss Linton. I very much doubt he'll be welcomed back.”
“And does Miss Linton give him the cold shoulder?” was the doctor's next question.
“She doesn't confide in me,” I replied, unwilling to discuss it further.

“No, she's a sly one,” he said, shaking his head. “She keeps her secrets! But she's a proper little fool. I've heard from a reliable source that last night—and a fine night it was for it!—she and Heathcliff walked for more than two hours in the plantation behind your house. He urged her not to go back inside, but to get on his horse and ride away with him! The person who told me said she could only put him off by giving her word of honour that she'd be ready the next time they met. When that was to be, he didn't hear. But you tell Mr. Linton to keep his eyes open!”

This news filled me with fresh alarm. I hurried ahead of Kenneth and ran most of the way home. The little dog was still yelping in the garden. I stopped a moment to open the gate for it, but instead of going to the house it raced about sniffing the grass, and would have escaped into the road if I had not caught it and carried it inside. Upstairs, Isabella's empty bedroom confirmed my suspicions. Had I been a few hours earlier, Mrs. Linton's illness might have stopped her from taking this rash step. But what could be done now? There was a faint chance of catching them if someone went after them at once. _I_ could not go, however, and I dared not wake the household and throw everyone into confusion. Still less could I tell my master: he was entirely taken up with his present trouble, with no strength left to bear another grief! I could see no choice but to hold my tongue and let events take their course. Kenneth had now arrived, and I went to announce him, scarcely able to compose my face. Catherine was sleeping uneasily. Her husband had managed to calm the worst of her frenzy and now bent over her pillow, watching every passing expression on her painfully expressive face.

After examining her himself, the doctor told him hopefully that she might recover if we could keep everything around her perfectly and continuously peaceful. To me he indicated that the greatest danger was not so much death as the permanent loss of her reason.

Neither Mr. Linton nor I closed our eyes that night. Indeed, neither of us went to bed. All the servants were up long before their usual time, moving quietly through the house and whispering whenever their work brought them together. Everyone was busy except Miss Isabella, and they began to comment on how soundly she was sleeping. Her brother also asked whether she was up. He seemed impatient for her to appear, and hurt that she showed so little concern for her sister-in-law. I trembled lest he send me to call her, but I was spared the pain of being the first to announce her flight. One of the maids, a thoughtless girl sent on an early errand to Gimmerton, came panting upstairs, burst open-mouthed into the bedroom, and cried, “Oh, dear, dear! What shall we have next? Master, master, our young lady—”
“Stop that noise!” I cried at once, furious at her shouting.
“Lower your voice, Mary. What's happened?” Mr. Linton said. “What's wrong with your young lady?”
“She's gone, she's gone! That Heathcliff's run off wi' her!” the girl gasped.
“That's not true!” Linton cried, getting up in distress. “It can't be. Where did you get such an idea? Ellen Dean, go and find her. It's unbelievable. It cannot be.”
While speaking, he took the maid to the door and again demanded to know what grounds she had for saying such a thing.

“Well, I met the lad who brings milk here on the road,” she stammered, “and he asked if there wasn't trouble at the Grange. I thought he meant the mistress being ill, so I said yes. Then he says, ‘Someone's gone after them, I suppose?’ I stared at him.
