The boy found plenty of energy to discuss Hareton's faults and shortcomings and tell stories about his behaviour. The girl enjoyed his cheeky, spiteful remarks without considering the unkindness they revealed. I began to dislike Linton more than I pitied him, and to excuse his father to some degree for thinking so little of him.

We stayed until afternoon; I could not get Miss Cathy away sooner. Luckily my master had not left his room and knew nothing of our long absence. On the walk home I tried to explain the characters of the people we had just left. But she had decided I was prejudiced against them.

“Aha!” she cried. “You take papa's side, Ellen. I know you're biased, or you wouldn't have deceived me all these years into thinking Linton lived far away. I'm really very angry, only I'm too pleased to show it! But you must keep quiet about my uncle. Remember, he's _my_ uncle, and I'll scold papa for quarrelling with him.”

She went on like this until I gave up trying to show her she was mistaken. She said nothing about the visit that evening, because she didn't see Mr. Linton. Next day it all came out, much to my dismay. Still, I wasn't entirely sorry. I thought he would guide and warn her more effectively than I could. But he was too hesitant about explaining fully why he wanted her to avoid everyone at the Heights, and Catherine demanded good reasons for anything that checked her indulged will.

“Papa!” she exclaimed after greeting him that morning. “Guess who I met on the moors yesterday. Ah, papa, you jumped! You haven't behaved properly, have you? I saw—but listen, and I'll tell you how I found you out. And Ellen too, who's been in league with you while pretending to feel so sorry for me whenever I hoped Linton would return and was disappointed again!”

She gave an accurate account of her outing and what followed. My master cast several reproachful glances at me but said nothing until she finished. Then he drew her close and asked whether she knew why he had hidden the fact that Linton lived nearby. Could she think he wanted to deny her a pleasure that would do her no harm?
“It was because you disliked Mr. Heathcliff,” she replied.

“Then you believe my own feelings matter more to me than yours, Cathy?” he said. “No. It wasn't because I dislike Mr. Heathcliff, but because he dislikes me. He's a devilish man who delights in hurting and ruining people he hates whenever they give him the slightest chance. I knew you couldn't remain friends with your cousin without meeting him, and I knew he would hate you because of me. So I took care to prevent your seeing Linton again entirely for your own good. I meant to explain when you were older, and I'm sorry I waited.”

“But Mr. Heathcliff was very friendly, papa,” Catherine said, quite unconvinced. “_He_ didn't object to our seeing each other. He said I could visit whenever I liked, only I mustn't tell you because you'd quarrelled with him and wouldn't forgive him for marrying Aunt Isabella. And you won't. _You're_ the one to blame. At least he's willing to let _us_ be friends, Linton and me, and you aren't.”

Seeing that she would not simply accept his word about her uncle by marriage, my master briefly described Heathcliff's treatment of Isabella and how he had acquired Wuthering Heights. He could not bear to discuss it for long. Though he rarely spoke of it, he still felt the same horror and hatred of his old enemy that had filled his heart since Mrs. Linton's death. “She might still be alive if it weren't for him!” was his constant bitter thought. In his eyes, Heathcliff was a murderer. Miss Cathy knew no wrongdoing beyond her own small acts of disobedience, unfairness, and anger, born of a hot temper and thoughtlessness and regretted the same day. She was astonished that a mind could be so dark as to brood secretly over revenge for years and deliberately carry out its plans without remorse. This new picture of human nature, absent until now from everything she had studied or imagined, seemed to shock her so deeply that Mr. Edgar thought further explanation unnecessary. He only added, “Later you'll understand, darling, why I want you to avoid his house and family. For now, go back to your usual work and pleasures, and think no more about them.”

Catherine kissed her father and quietly settled to her lessons for the usual couple of hours. Afterwards she walked with him in the grounds, and the day passed as normal. But that evening, when I went to her room to help her undress, I found her kneeling beside the bed in tears.

“Oh, shame, you silly child!” I cried. “If you had real troubles, you'd be ashamed to waste a tear over this little disappointment. You've never known even the shadow of genuine sorrow, Miss Catherine. Imagine for a moment that your father and I were dead and you were alone in the world. How would you feel then? Compare this with a grief like that, and be grateful for the friends you have instead of wanting more.”
“I'm not crying for myself, Ellen,” she answered. “I'm crying for him. He expects to see me tomorrow, and he'll be so disappointed. He'll wait for me, and I won't come!”

“Nonsense!” I said. “Do you think he's thought about you as much as you've thought about him? Doesn't he have Hareton for company? Not one person in a hundred would cry over losing a relation they'd only seen twice, for two afternoons. Linton will guess what's happened and think no more about you.”

“But couldn't I write a note explaining why I can't come?” she asked, getting up. “And send the books I promised to lend him? His aren't as nice as mine, and when I told him how interesting mine were, he wanted them very much. Couldn't I, Ellen?”

“No, indeed! Certainly not!” I replied firmly. “Then he'd write back, and it would never end. No, Miss Catherine, you must have no more contact with him. That's what papa expects, and I'll make sure of it.”
“But how could one little note—?” she began again, putting on a pleading expression.
“Be quiet!” I interrupted. “We aren't starting with your little notes. Get into bed.”

She gave me such a naughty look that at first I refused to kiss her good night. I tucked her in and closed the door, thoroughly displeased. Halfway away, though, I relented and went quietly back. And there she was, standing at the table with a sheet of blank paper before her and a pencil in her hand! She guiltily hid the pencil as I entered.
“If you write that, Catherine, you won't find anyone to deliver it,” I said. “And now I'm putting out your candle.”

I lowered the snuffer over the flame and received a slap on the hand and an angry “Cross thing!” for my pains. Then I left again, and she bolted the door in one of her worst, most petulant moods. She finished the letter and sent it through a boy who collected milk for the village, though I did not discover that until later. Weeks passed, and Cathy's good temper returned. But she became remarkably fond of slipping into corners alone. If I suddenly approached while she was reading, she often started and bent over her book, plainly trying to hide it. I noticed loose sheets of paper sticking out between the pages. She also took to coming downstairs early and lingering in the kitchen, as though expecting something to arrive. She had a small drawer in a library cabinet over which she would spend hours, and she was particularly careful to take its key whenever she left.

One day, while she was looking through the drawer, I saw that the toys and trinkets it had lately held had turned into folded pieces of paper. Curious and suspicious, I decided to examine these mysterious treasures. That night, once she and my master were safely upstairs, I searched among my household keys and easily found one that fitted. I opened the drawer, emptied everything into my apron, and carried it to my own room to inspect at leisure. Despite my suspicions, I was still surprised to find a mass of letters from Linton Heathcliff. They must have written almost daily: these were replies to letters she had sent him. The earliest were awkward and short. Gradually they became lengthy love letters, as foolish as the writer's age made natural, yet with occasional touches I thought borrowed from someone more experienced. Some struck me as very strange mixtures of passion and dullness, beginning with strong feeling and ending in the affected, wordy style a schoolboy might use to an imaginary sweetheart. Whether they satisfied Cathy I cannot say. To me they seemed worthless rubbish. After reading as many as I thought necessary, I tied them in a handkerchief, set them aside, and locked the empty drawer again.

As usual, my young lady came down early and went to the kitchen. I watched her go to the door when a certain little boy arrived. While the dairymaid filled his can, Cathy slipped something into his jacket pocket and took something out. I went round through the garden and waited for the messenger. He fought bravely to protect his charge, and between us we spilt the milk, but I managed to seize the letter. After threatening dire consequences unless he hurried home, I stayed beside the wall and read Miss Cathy's affectionate composition. It was simpler and more eloquent than her cousin's, very pretty and very silly. I shook my head and went thoughtfully indoors. Since it was raining, she couldn't amuse herself in the park. When her morning lessons ended, she turned to the drawer for comfort. Her father sat reading at the table, and I had deliberately found work repairing some loose curtain fringe so I could keep watch. No bird returning to a robbed nest it had left full of chirping young could have shown greater despair in its cries and fluttering than she showed in one “Oh!” and the transformation of her previously happy face. Mr. Linton looked up.
“What's wrong, love? Have you hurt yourself?” he asked.
His voice and expression reassured her that _he_ had not found her treasure.
“No, papa!” she gasped. “Ellen! Ellen! Come upstairs. I feel ill!”
I did as she asked and went out with her.

“Oh, Ellen! You've got them,” she began at once, falling to her knees as soon as we were alone. “Oh, give them back, and I'll never, never do it again! Don't tell papa. You haven't told him, Ellen? Say you haven't! I've been terribly naughty, but I won't do it any more!”
With a solemn, stern manner I ordered her to stand.

“So, Miss Catherine,” I exclaimed, “you seem to have gone quite far! You ought to be ashamed of them. What a fine bundle of rubbish you study in your spare time—good enough to print! What do you think the master will say when I show it to him? I haven't yet, but don't imagine I'll keep your ridiculous secrets. Shame on you! You must have started writing this nonsense. I'm sure he wouldn't have thought of it first.”
“I didn't! I didn't!” Cathy sobbed as though her heart would break. “I never thought of loving him until—”

“_Loving_!” I cried, putting all the scorn I could into the word. “_Loving_! Who ever heard of such a thing! I might as well talk of loving the miller who comes once a year to buy our grain. Fine love, indeed! You've barely spent four hours with Linton in your life, counting both visits! Now, here's the childish nonsense. I'm taking it to the library, and we'll see what your father thinks of such _love_.”

She sprang towards her precious letters, but I held them above my head. Then she begged frantically that I burn them, do anything rather than show them. I was really as inclined to laugh as to scold, since I considered it all girlish vanity. At last I softened a little and asked, “If I agree to burn them, will you solemnly promise never to send or receive another letter, or a book—I see you've sent him books—or locks of hair, rings, or toys?”
“We don't send toys,” Catherine cried, her pride getting the better of her shame.
“Nor anything at all, then, my lady?” I said. “Unless you promise, I'm going.”
“I promise, Ellen!” she cried, catching my dress. “Oh, put them in the fire, please, please!”
But when I began making a space in the fire with the poker, the sacrifice became too painful to bear. She begged me earnestly to spare one or two.
“One or two, Ellen, to keep for Linton's sake!”
I untied the handkerchief and began tipping them into the fire from one corner. Flames curled up the chimney.
“I will have one, you cruel wretch!” she screamed. She plunged her hand into the fire and pulled out some half-burnt scraps, burning her fingers in the process.
“Very well, then I'll keep some to show papa!” I answered. I shook the rest back into the bundle and turned towards the door again.

She dropped her blackened scraps into the flames and motioned for me to finish the sacrifice. I did so, stirred the ashes, and buried them beneath a shovelful of coal. Silent and feeling deeply wronged, she went to her own room. I went downstairs and told my master that the young lady's sudden sickness had almost passed, but I thought she should lie down for a while. She refused dinner. At tea she reappeared, pale and red-eyed, with an outward meekness quite unlike her. Next morning I answered the letter with a slip of paper: “Master Heathcliff is asked to send no more notes to Miss Linton, as she will not accept them.” After that, the little boy's pockets came empty.

chapters.title: Chapter XXII
paragraphs: Summer ended, followed by early autumn. Michaelmas had passed, but the harvest was late that year and a few fields still stood uncut. Mr. Linton and his daughter often walked out among the reapers. When the last sheaves were being brought in, they stayed until dusk. The evening was cold and damp, and my master caught a bad cold that settled stubbornly on his lungs and kept him indoors almost continuously throughout the winter.

Poor Cathy, frightened into giving up her little romance, had been much sadder and quieter since it ended. Her father insisted that she read less and exercise more. Since he could no longer walk with her, I felt it my duty to replace his company with mine as far as possible. I was a poor substitute: with all my daily work, I could spare only two or three hours to accompany her, and she clearly preferred his company to mine.

One afternoon in October or early November, I asked her to give up her walk because I was certain it would rain. It was a cool, watery afternoon; wet, dead leaves rustled over the grass and paths, and dark grey streaks of cloud were racing up from the west, half covering the cold blue sky and promising heavy rain. She refused, so I reluctantly put on a cloak, took my umbrella, and went with her towards the lower end of the park. She usually chose that orderly path when she was low in spirits, as she always was when Mr. Edgar was worse than usual. He never admitted it, but she and I guessed from his increased silence and the sadness of his face. She walked sorrowfully, without running or skipping, though the cold wind might well have encouraged a race. Often, out of the corner of my eye, I saw her raise a hand and brush something from her cheek. I looked about for a way to distract her. Beside the road rose a steep, rough bank where hazels and stunted oaks clung precariously, their roots half exposed. The soil was too loose for the oaks, and strong winds had pushed some almost horizontal. In summer Miss Catherine loved climbing along their trunks and sitting in the branches, swinging twenty feet above the ground. Delighted as I was by her nimbleness and carefree childish heart, I still thought it proper to scold whenever I found her so high up—but in a way that told her she needn't come down. Between dinner and tea she would lie in her cradle rocked by the breeze, singing old songs I had taught her in the nursery, or watching the birds who shared it feed their young and coax them into flight. Or she would nestle there with her eyes shut, half thinking, half dreaming, happier than words could express.

“Look, Miss!” I cried, pointing beneath the roots of a twisted tree. “Winter hasn't arrived yet. There's a little flower up there, the last bloom of all those bluebells that covered the grassy steps with a lilac mist in July. Will you climb up and pick it for papa?”
Cathy gazed for a long time at the lonely flower trembling in its little shelter of earth. At last she said, “No, I won't touch it. But it looks sad, doesn't it, Ellen?”
“Yes,” I remarked, “about as chilled and drooping as you. There's no colour in your cheeks. Let's hold hands and run. You're so listless, I daresay I'll keep up.”

“No,” she repeated, and kept walking slowly. Now and then she stopped to contemplate some moss, a tuft of faded grass, or a bright orange fungus spreading among heaps of brown leaves. Every so often her hand went up to her turned-away face.
“Catherine, why are you crying, love?” I asked, coming close and putting my arm round her shoulders. “You mustn't cry because papa has a cold. Be thankful it's nothing worse.”
Now she stopped trying to control her tears. Sobs choked her breath.

“Oh, it _will_ become something worse,” she said. “What will I do when papa and you leave me and I'm all alone? I can't forget what you said, Ellen. I hear it all the time. How different life will be, how dreary the world, when you and papa are dead.”

“Nobody knows whether you might die before us,” I replied. “It's wrong to expect trouble in advance. Let's hope we all have years and years ahead. Your father is young, and I'm strong and barely forty-five. My mother lived to eighty and was a lively woman to the end. Suppose Mr. Linton lives to sixty: that would leave him more years than you've lived yourself, Miss. Wouldn't it be foolish to mourn a disaster more than twenty years before it happens?”
“But Aunt Isabella was younger than papa,” she said, looking up with timid hope for further comfort.

“Aunt Isabella didn't have you and me to nurse her,” I replied. “She wasn't as happy as your father and had less to live for. All you need to do is care for him properly, cheer him by being cheerful yourself, and avoid giving him anything to worry about. Remember that, Cathy! I won't hide it from you: you might kill him if you behaved wildly and recklessly, nursing some foolish romantic fancy for the son of a man who'd be glad to see him in his grave, and let him discover that you were grieving over the separation he thought necessary.”

“Nothing in the world worries me except papa's illness,” she answered. “Nothing matters beside papa. And I'll never—never—oh, never, as long as I have my senses, do or say anything to upset him. I love him more than myself, Ellen, and this is how I know: every night I pray to outlive him, because I'd rather suffer than have him suffer. That proves I love him more than myself.”
“Fine words,” I replied. “But your actions must prove it too. When he's well again, don't forget the promises you made while you were afraid.”

As we talked, we approached a door in the wall opening on to the road. My young lady's spirits brightened again. She climbed up and sat on the wall, reaching for scarlet rosehips on the highest branches of the wild roses overhanging the roadside. All the lower fruit had gone; only birds could reach what was left unless they sat where Cathy was. As she stretched for them, her hat fell off. Since the door was locked, she proposed climbing down to fetch it. I warned her not to fall, and she nimbly disappeared. Getting back was another matter. The stones were smooth and neatly mortared, and neither the roses nor the trailing brambles could help her climb. Foolishly, I didn't remember this until I heard her laughing and calling, “Ellen! You'll have to fetch the key, or I'll have to run round to the lodge. I can't scale the battlements from this side!”
“Stay there,” I answered. “I've got my keys in my pocket. Perhaps one will open it. If not, I'll go.”

Catherine amused herself by dancing back and forth outside the door while I tried the larger keys one after another. The last failed like the rest. I told her again to stay where she was and was about to hurry home as fast as possible when an approaching sound stopped me: a horse trotting. Cathy stopped dancing too.
“Who is it?” I whispered.
“Ellen, I wish you could open the door,” she whispered back anxiously.
“Hello, Miss Linton!” the rider's deep voice called. “I'm glad I've met you. Don't hurry inside. I want an explanation from you, and I mean to have it.”
“I won't speak to you, Mr. Heathcliff,” Catherine answered. “Papa says you're a wicked man and you hate us both. Ellen says so too.”

“That's beside the point,” Heathcliff said—for it was he. “I don't hate my son, presumably, and it's about him that you must listen. Yes, you've reason to blush. Two or three months ago you were writing to Linton, weren't you? Playing at love, eh? You both deserved a whipping for that! Especially you, being older and, as it turns out, less sensitive. I have your letters, and if you're impertinent I'll send them to your father. I suppose you grew bored with the amusement and gave it up? Well, when you dropped it, you dropped Linton into a slough of despair. He was serious, truly in love. As surely as I live, he's dying for you, his heart breaking because you've changed. Not in a manner of speaking: actually breaking. Hareton has mocked him constantly for six weeks, and I've tried stronger measures, trying to frighten him out of his foolishness. But he grows worse every day. Unless you bring him back to life, he'll be in his grave before summer!”

“How can you tell that poor child such blatant lies?” I called from inside the wall. “Please ride on! How can you deliberately invent such contemptible falsehoods? Miss Cathy, I'll break the lock with a stone. Don't believe that vile nonsense. Your own heart can tell you that nobody could die of love for a stranger.”

“I didn't realise anyone was listening,” the exposed villain muttered. Then, louder: “Worthy Mrs. Dean, I like you, but I don't like your deceit. How could _you_ tell such blatant lies as to say I hated the ‘poor child’, and invent bogey stories to frighten her away from my doorstep? Catherine Linton—the very name warms my heart—my bonny lass, I'll be away all week. Go and see whether I've told the truth. Do, there's a darling! Imagine your father in my place and Linton in yours. What would you think of your careless lover if he wouldn't take a single step to comfort you, even when your father himself begged him? Don't be stupid enough to make the same mistake. I swear by my salvation that he's going to his grave, and only you can save him!”
The lock broke, and I came out.

“I swear Linton is dying,” Heathcliff repeated, staring hard at me. “Grief and disappointment are hurrying his death. Nelly, if you won't let her go, you can walk over yourself. But I won't be back until this time next week, and I scarcely think even your master would object to her visiting her cousin.”
“Come inside,” I said, taking Cathy by the arm and half forcing her through the door. She lingered, looking anxiously at his face, whose sternness gave away none of the deception beneath.
He urged his horse closer, bent down, and said:

“Miss Catherine, I'll admit I have little patience with Linton, and Hareton and Joseph have less. I'll admit he's among harsh people. He longs for kindness as well as love, and a kind word from you would be his best medicine. Ignore Mrs. Dean's cruel warnings. Be generous and find a way to see him. He dreams of you night and day, and because you neither visit nor write, nothing can persuade him that you don't hate him.”

I shut the door and rolled a stone against it to help the damaged lock hold. Opening my umbrella, I drew Cathy beneath it. Rain was beginning to drive through the moaning branches, warning us to hurry. We said nothing of Heathcliff as we hastened home, but I instinctively knew that a double darkness now weighed on Catherine's heart. Her face was so sad it scarcely looked like hers. Plainly she believed every word he had said.

The master had gone to bed before we returned. Cathy slipped into his room to ask how he was, but he was asleep. She came back and asked me to sit with her in the library. We had tea together. Afterwards she lay on the rug and asked me not to talk, saying she was tired. I took a book and pretended to read. Once she thought I was absorbed, she began silently crying again; it seemed to be her favourite occupation just then. I let her indulge it for a while, then protested, mocking and ridiculing everything Mr. Heathcliff had said about his son as though I were sure she would agree. Alas! I had no skill to undo the effect of his story. It had worked exactly as he intended.
“You may be right, Ellen,” she answered, “but I won't have any peace until I know. And I must tell Linton it isn't my fault I don't write, and make him understand I won't change.”

What good were anger and protests against her foolish willingness to believe him? We parted that night on hostile terms. Yet next day I was on the road to Wuthering Heights beside my wilful young mistress's pony. I couldn't bear her grief, her pale, dejected face and heavy eyes. I gave in, faintly hoping that Linton's own welcome would show how little truth there was in the story.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIII
paragraphs: The wet night gave way to a misty morning, half frost and half drizzle. Temporary streams gurgled down from the high ground and crossed our path. My feet were soaked, and I was irritable and miserable, in exactly the mood to dwell on every discomfort. We entered the farmhouse through the kitchen to find out whether Mr. Heathcliff was really away, since I put little trust in his word.

Joseph sat alone in what seemed his own private paradise beside a roaring fire. A quart of ale stood nearby, bristling with large pieces of toasted oatcake, and a short black pipe was in his mouth. Catherine hurried to the hearth to warm herself. I asked whether the master was home. He left me unanswered so long that I thought he had gone deaf and repeated the question louder.
“Na-ay!” he snarled, or rather screeched through his nose. “Na-ay! Ye can go back where ye came from.”
“Joseph!” a fretful voice called from the inner room at the same moment as mine. “How many times must I call you? There's nothing left but a few glowing ashes. Joseph! Come here this instant.”

Vigorous puffs on his pipe and a fixed stare into the fire announced that Joseph heard none of it. Neither the housekeeper nor Hareton was to be seen, probably out on an errand and at work respectively. We recognised Linton's voice and went in.
“Oh, I hope you die in an attic, frozen to death!” the boy said, mistaking our footsteps for those of his neglectful servant.
He stopped when he saw his mistake. His cousin rushed to him.

“Is that you, Miss Linton?” he asked, lifting his head from the arm of the large chair in which he lay. “No, don't kiss me. I can't breathe. Dear me! Papa said you'd come,” he continued once he had recovered a little from Catherine's embrace. She stood beside him, looking very sorry. “Would you please shut the door? You left it open. And those—those _hateful_ creatures won't bring coal. It's so cold!”

I stirred the dying fire and fetched a scuttle of coal myself. The sick boy complained that I had covered him with ashes, but his persistent cough and feverish, ill appearance stopped me from rebuking his temper.
“Well, Linton,” Catherine murmured when his frown relaxed, “are you glad I've come? Can I do anything to help you?”

“Why didn't you come sooner?” he asked. “You should have visited instead of writing. Those long letters tired me terribly. I'd much rather have talked to you. Now I can't bear talking, or anything else. Where can Zillah be! Will you”—he looked at me—“go into the kitchen and see?”
He had given me no thanks for fetching the coal. Unwilling to run back and forth at his command, I answered:
“There's nobody out there except Joseph.”

“I want a drink,” he exclaimed fretfully, turning away. “Since papa left, Zillah is always off gadding about in Gimmerton. It's miserable! And I have to come down here because they've decided not to hear me when I'm upstairs.”
“Does your father look after you, Master Heathcliff?” I asked, seeing Catherine discouraged in her attempts at kindness.

“Look after me? At least he makes _them_ do a little more,” he cried. “The wretches! Do you know, Miss Linton, that brute Hareton laughs at me! I hate him! In fact, I hate all of them. They're horrible creatures.”

Cathy looked for water, found a jug on the dresser, filled a glass, and brought it to him. He told her to add a spoonful of wine from the bottle on the table. After swallowing a little, he seemed calmer and told her she was very kind.
“And are you glad to see me?” she asked again, pleased to notice the first faint sign of a smile.

“Yes, I am. Hearing a voice like yours makes a change!” he replied. “But I've been upset because you wouldn't come. Papa swore it was my fault. He called me a pitiful, shifty, worthless thing and said you despised me. He said that in my place he'd be more master of the Grange than your father by now. But you don't despise me, do you, Miss—?”

“I wish you'd call me Catherine, or Cathy,” my young lady interrupted. “Despise you? No! Except for papa and Ellen, I love you more than anyone alive. But I don't love Mr. Heathcliff, and I daren't come when he's back. Will he be away for many days?”

“Not many,” Linton answered. “But since the shooting season began, he's often out on the moors. You could spend an hour or two with me while he's gone. Do say you will. I don't think I'd be bad-tempered with you. You wouldn't provoke me, and you'd always be willing to help, wouldn't you?”
“Yes,” Catherine said, stroking his long, soft hair. “If only papa would agree, I'd spend half my time with you. Pretty Linton! I wish you were my brother.”
“Then you'd love me as much as your father?” he said more cheerfully. “But papa says if you were my wife you'd love me more than him and everyone else, so I'd rather you were that.”

“No, I'll never love anyone more than papa,” she answered seriously. “And sometimes people hate their wives, but they don't hate their brothers and sisters. If you were my brother, you'd live with us, and papa would love you as much as me.”

Linton denied that anyone ever hated his wife. Cathy insisted they did and, in her wisdom, gave his father's hatred of her aunt as an example. I tried to stop her thoughtless tongue, but couldn't until she had told everything she knew. Master Heathcliff, deeply irritated, declared her account untrue.
“Papa told me, and papa doesn't tell lies,” she answered sharply.
“_My_ papa despises yours!” Linton cried. “He calls him a sneaking fool.”
“Yours is a wicked man,” Catherine retorted, “and you're very naughty to repeat what he says. He must be wicked, or Aunt Isabella wouldn't have left him as she did.”
“She didn't leave him,” the boy said. “You mustn't contradict me.”
“Yes, she did,” my young lady cried.
“Well, I'll tell _you_ something!” Linton said. “Your mother hated your father. There!”
“Oh!” Catherine exclaimed, too furious to say more.
“And she loved mine,” he added.
“You little liar! Now I hate you!” she gasped, her face flushing with rage.
“She did! She did!” Linton chanted, sinking back in his chair and tilting his head to enjoy the distress of his opponent, who stood behind him.
“Be quiet, Master Heathcliff!” I said. “I suppose that's another story from your father.”
“It isn't. You keep quiet!” he answered. “She did, she did, Catherine! She did, she did!”

Beside herself, Cathy shoved the chair violently and knocked him against one of its arms. A choking fit of coughing immediately ended his triumph. It went on so long that even I grew frightened. His cousin cried desperately, horrified by the harm she had done, but said nothing. I supported him until the fit wore itself out. Then he pushed me away and bowed his head in silence. Catherine also stopped crying, sat opposite him, and stared gravely into the fire.
“How do you feel now, Master Heathcliff?” I asked after waiting ten minutes.
“I wish _she_ felt like this,” he replied. “Spiteful, cruel thing! Hareton never touches me. He's never hit me in his life. And I was better today, and now—” His voice faded into a whimper.
“_I_ didn't hit you!” Cathy muttered, biting her lip to keep from breaking down again.

He sighed and moaned like someone in terrible pain, keeping it up for a quarter of an hour. Apparently he meant to distress his cousin: whenever he heard her suppress a sob, he put fresh suffering and sorrow into his voice.

“I'm sorry I hurt you, Linton,” she said at last, tormented beyond endurance. “But that little push couldn't have hurt _me_, and I never imagined it could hurt you either. You aren't badly hurt, are you, Linton? Don't let me go home thinking I've harmed you. Answer me! Please speak.”

“I can't talk to you,” he murmured. “You've hurt me so badly I'll be awake all night, choking with this cough. If you had it, you'd know what it was like. But _you'll_ sleep comfortably while I'm in agony with nobody near me. I wonder how you'd like spending such dreadful nights!” And he began wailing aloud out of sheer pity for himself.

“If you regularly have dreadful nights,” I said, “Miss Cathy can't be the one spoiling your rest. You'd be just the same if she'd never come. However, she won't disturb you again. Perhaps you'll settle down once we leave.”
“Must I go?” Catherine asked sadly, bending over him. “Do you want me to leave, Linton?”
“You can't undo what's happened,” he said peevishly, shrinking away, “unless you make it worse by pestering me into a fever.”
“Then I must go?” she repeated.
“At least leave me alone,” he said. “I can't stand your talking.”

She lingered for an exhausting length of time, resisting my efforts to take her away. But he neither looked up nor spoke, and at last she moved towards the door, with me following. A scream brought us back. Linton had slid from his chair on to the hearthstone and lay writhing with what I took to be the sheer wilfulness of a spoiled, troublesome child determined to be as distressing and tiresome as possible. His behaviour showed me exactly what his disposition was, and I saw that humouring him would be foolish. My companion thought otherwise. Terrified, she ran back, knelt, cried, soothed, and begged until he quieted from lack of breath, certainly not from any regret at upsetting her.

“I'll put him on the bench,” I said, “and he can roll about as much as he likes. We can't stay to watch. I hope you see now, Miss Cathy, that _you_ aren't the person to do him good, and his illness isn't caused by his love for you. There, now! Come away. Once he knows nobody's here to mind his nonsense, he'll be glad to lie still.”
She slipped a cushion beneath his head and offered him water. He refused the water and tossed uncomfortably against the cushion as though it were stone or wood. She tried to arrange it better.
“That won't do,” he said. “It isn't high enough.”
Catherine fetched another cushion and put it on top.
“That's _too_ high,” the provoking creature murmured.
“Then how shall I put it?” she asked in despair.
As she half knelt beside the bench, he curled up against her and rested on her shoulder.
“No, that won't do,” I said. “You'll have to manage with the cushion, Master Heathcliff. Miss has wasted too much time on you already. We can't stay another five minutes.”

“Yes, yes, we can!” Cathy answered. “He's being good and patient now. He's beginning to understand how much more miserable than him I'll be tonight if I think my visit has made him worse. Then I wouldn't dare come again. Tell the truth, Linton. If I've hurt you, I mustn't come.”
“You must come to make me well,” he replied. “You ought to, because you've hurt me. You know you've hurt me badly! I wasn't as ill when you arrived as I am now, was I?”
“But you've made yourself ill by crying and getting angry. I didn't do it all,” his cousin said. “Still, let's be friends now. And you do want me? You really would like to see me sometimes?”

“I told you I did,” he replied impatiently. “Sit on the bench and let me rest on your lap. Mamma used to do that for whole afternoons. Sit perfectly still and don't talk. But you may sing if you can, or recite a good long ballad, one of those you promised to teach me, or tell a story. I'd rather have a ballad, though. Begin.”

Catherine recited the longest one she could remember. It pleased them both immensely. Linton wanted another, then another, despite my strong objections. They continued until the clock struck twelve and we heard Hareton returning through the yard for dinner.
“And tomorrow, Catherine? Will you come tomorrow?” young Heathcliff asked, holding her dress as she reluctantly rose.
“No,” I answered, “and not the day after either.” But she evidently gave a different answer: when she bent to whisper in his ear, his frown cleared.
“Remember, Miss, you aren't going tomorrow!” I began once we were outside. “You're not thinking of it, are you?”
She gave a smile.
“Oh, I'll see to it,” I went on. “I'll have that lock repaired, and there's no other way out.”

“I can climb the wall,” she said, laughing. “The Grange isn't a prison, Ellen, and you aren't my jailer. Besides, I'm nearly seventeen. I'm a woman. I'm certain Linton would soon recover if I looked after him. You know I'm older than him, and wiser, less childish, aren't I? With a little coaxing he'd soon do as I tell him. He's such a pretty little darling when he's good. If he were mine, I'd spoil him with affection. Once we were used to each other, we'd never quarrel, would we? Don't you like him, Ellen?”

“Like him!” I exclaimed. “The most bad-tempered scrap of a sickly boy that ever struggled into his teens. Luckily, as Mr. Heathcliff guessed, he won't reach twenty. Indeed, I doubt he'll see spring. Whenever he dies, his family will suffer little loss. It's lucky for us his father took him. The kinder people were to him, the more tiresome and selfish he'd become. I'm glad you have no chance of marrying him, Miss Catherine.”
My companion grew serious at this speech. My careless talk of his death hurt her feelings.

“He's younger than me,” she answered after a long, thoughtful pause, “so he ought to live longer. He will—he must live as long as I do. He's as strong now as when he first came north. I'm sure of it. It's only a cold, like papa's. You say papa will get better. Why shouldn't he?”

“Well, well,” I cried, “we needn't trouble ourselves about it. Listen, Miss, and remember I'll keep my word: if you try to go to Wuthering Heights again, with me or without me, I'll tell Mr. Linton. Unless he gives permission, you mustn't renew your friendship with your cousin.”
“It's already renewed,” Cathy muttered sulkily.
“Then you mustn't continue it,” I said.
“We'll see,” she answered, then set off at a gallop, leaving me to struggle along behind.

We both reached home before dinner. My master assumed we had been walking in the park and asked no questions about our absence. I hurried to change my soaking shoes and stockings as soon as I entered, but sitting so long at the Heights had done the damage. Next morning I was confined to bed. For three weeks I couldn't attend to my duties, something that had never happened before and, I'm thankful to say, has never happened since.

My little mistress was an angel, coming to nurse me and brighten my lonely hours. Being shut indoors made me very low; it's wearisome for an active person. But few people could have had less cause to complain than I did. The moment Catherine left Mr. Linton's room, she appeared at my bedside. She divided her day between us, giving not a minute to amusement. She neglected meals, lessons, and play, and was the most affectionate nurse anyone could have. She must have had a warm heart to spare so much love for me when she loved her father so deeply. I said her days were divided between us, but the master went to bed early, and I generally needed nothing after six, so her evenings were her own. Poor thing! I never considered what she did after tea. Often, when she came to say good night, I noticed fresh colour in her cheeks and a pink glow over her slender fingers. Instead of imagining it came from a cold ride across the moors, I blamed a hot fire in the library.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIV
paragraphs: After three weeks I could leave my bedroom and move around the house. The first evening I was well enough to stay up, I asked Catherine to read to me, because my eyes were still weak. We were in the library, and the master had gone to bed. She agreed, though I thought she seemed reluctant. Supposing my books were not to her taste, I told her to choose anything she liked. She picked one of her favourites and read steadily for about an hour. Then the questions began.
“Ellen, aren't you tired? Wouldn't you be better off lying down now? You'll make yourself ill, staying up so long, Ellen.”
“No, no, dear, I'm not tired,” I kept answering.
When she saw that I would not move, she tried another way of showing how little she enjoyed her task. She began yawning and stretching, and then said—
“Ellen, I'm tired.”
“Stop reading, then, and talk to me,” I said.

That was worse. She fidgeted and sighed and kept checking her watch until eight. At last she went to her room, apparently quite overcome with sleep, judging by her heavy, irritable expression and the way she constantly rubbed her eyes. The next evening she was even more restless. On the third evening after I had rejoined her, she complained of a headache and left me. Her behaviour puzzled me. After sitting alone for a long time, I decided to see whether she felt better and invite her to lie on the sofa, instead of remaining upstairs in the dark. But Catherine was nowhere upstairs, or downstairs either. The servants said they had not seen her. I listened outside Mr. Edgar's door: everything was quiet. I went back to her room, put out my candle, and sat by the window.

The moon was bright, and a light dusting of snow covered the ground. Perhaps, I thought, she had taken it into her head to get some fresh air in the garden. I did see a figure slipping along the park's inner fence, but it was not my young mistress. When it came into the light, I recognised one of the grooms. He stood for some time watching the drive through the grounds, then suddenly hurried off as though he had spotted something. Soon he returned leading Miss Catherine's pony, with Catherine herself, just dismounted, walking beside it. The man quietly led the pony across the grass towards the stable. Cathy climbed through the drawing-room window and stole noiselessly upstairs to the room where I was waiting. She gently closed the door, slipped off her snowy shoes, and untied her hat. Still unaware that I was watching, she was taking off her cloak when I suddenly stood up and showed myself. For a moment the shock froze her. She made an inarticulate sound and stood perfectly still.

“My dear Miss Catherine,” I began, too mindful of her recent kindness to launch into a scolding, “where have you been riding at this time of night? And why did you try to deceive me with a story? Where have you been? Tell me!”
“To the bottom of the park,” she stammered. “I didn't tell you a story.”
“And nowhere else?” I insisted.
“No,” she muttered.

“Oh, Catherine!” I cried sadly. “You know you've been doing wrong, or you wouldn't be driven to lying to me. That really hurts me. I'd rather be ill for three months than hear you deliberately make up a lie.”
She rushed towards me, burst into tears, and flung her arms around my neck.
“Well, Ellen, I'm so frightened you'll be angry,” she said. “Promise you won't, and I'll tell you the whole truth. I hate keeping it hidden.”
We sat together on the window seat. I promised not to scold, whatever her secret was—though of course I had already guessed it—and she began.

“I've been going to Wuthering Heights, Ellen. Since you fell ill I've gone every day, except three times before you came downstairs and twice afterwards. I gave Michael books and pictures to have Minny ready every evening and put her back in the stable. Remember, you mustn't scold _him_ either. I reached the Heights by half past six, usually stayed until half past eight, and then galloped home. I didn't go just to enjoy myself. Often I was miserable the whole time. Now and then I was happy—perhaps once a week. At first I thought it would be terribly hard to persuade you to let me keep my promise to Linton: when we left him, I'd promised to visit again the next day. But you stayed upstairs that day, so I didn't have to persuade you. In the afternoon, while Michael was fixing the lock back onto the park gate, I got hold of the key. I told him my cousin wanted me to visit because he was ill and couldn't come to the Grange, and that papa would object to my going. Then I made an arrangement with him about the pony. He likes reading, and he's thinking of leaving soon to get married. He offered to do what I wanted if I lent him books from the library, but I preferred to give him my own, and he liked that even better.

“On my second visit Linton seemed quite cheerful. Zillah—their housekeeper—gave us a clean room and a good fire. She said Joseph was at a prayer meeting and Hareton Earnshaw was out with his dogs—stealing pheasants from our woods, I heard afterwards—so we could do as we pleased. She brought me warm wine and gingerbread and seemed wonderfully kind. Linton sat in the armchair, and I sat in the little rocking chair on the hearth. We laughed and talked so happily and found so much to say. We planned where we would go and what we would do in summer. I needn't repeat all that: you'd call it silly.

“But at one point we nearly quarrelled. He said the loveliest way to spend a hot July day was to lie from morning to evening on a bank of heather in the middle of the moors, with bees humming sleepily among the flowers, larks singing high overhead, and a blue sky and bright sun shining steadily without a cloud. That was his perfect idea of heavenly happiness. Mine was to sway in a rustling green tree, with a west wind blowing and brilliant white clouds racing above; and not just larks but thrushes, blackbirds, linnets, and cuckoos pouring out music everywhere. In the distance the moors would be broken by cool, shadowy valleys, and close by there would be great sweeps of long grass rolling in waves before the breeze, woods and the sound of water, and the whole world awake and wild with joy. He wanted everything to rest in an ecstasy of peace; I wanted everything to sparkle and dance in a glorious celebration. I said his heaven would be only half alive, and he said mine would be drunk. I said I'd fall asleep in his, and he said he couldn't breathe in mine, and grew quite snappish. At last we agreed to try both as soon as the weather was right. Then we kissed and made friends again.

“After sitting still for an hour, I looked at that big room with its smooth, bare floor and thought how lovely it would be to play there if we moved the table. I asked Linton to call Zillah to help us, and suggested blindman's buff, with her trying to catch us—you used to do that, Ellen, you know. He wouldn't. He said there was no fun in it, but he agreed to play ball with me. We found two balls in a cupboard among a heap of old toys: tops, hoops, battledores, and shuttlecocks. One had a C. on it, and the other an H. I wanted the C., for Catherine; the H. could stand for Heathcliff, his name. But the bran stuffing was coming out of H., and Linton didn't like that one. I kept beating him. He grew cross again, began coughing, and went back to his chair. That evening, though, it was easy to cheer him up. He loved two or three pretty songs I sang—_your_ songs, Ellen. When I had to leave, he begged and begged me to return the next evening, and I promised. Minny and I flew home as light as air, and all night I dreamt of Wuthering Heights and my sweet, darling cousin.

“The next day I was sad, partly because you were ill and partly because I wished my father knew about my visits and approved of them. But there was beautiful moonlight after tea, and as I rode along my gloom lifted. I'll have another happy evening, I thought, and what makes me happier still, my lovely Linton will too. I trotted up their garden and was turning towards the back when that fellow Earnshaw met me. He took my bridle and told me to go in at the front. He stroked Minny's neck, said she was a bonny beast, and seemed to want me to talk to him. I only told him to leave my horse alone or she would kick him. In his coarse accent he answered, ‘Wouldn't do much hurt if she did,’ and smiled as he looked at her legs. I was half tempted to make her try. But he moved away to open the door. As he lifted the latch, he looked up at the inscription above it and said, with a ridiculous mixture of awkwardness and pride, ‘Miss Catherine! I can read yon now.’
“‘How wonderful!’ I said. ‘Do let me hear you. You _have_ become clever!’
“He spelled out the name and laboured through it syllable by syllable: ‘Hareton Earnshaw.’
“‘And the numbers?’ I asked encouragingly, seeing that he had come to a complete stop.
“‘I can't make them out yet,’ he answered.
“‘Oh, you dunce!’ I said, laughing heartily at his failure.

“The fool stared at me, with something like a grin on his lips and a frown forming over his eyes. He seemed uncertain whether to laugh with me—whether I was being pleasantly familiar or showing what I really felt, contempt. I settled the question by suddenly becoming serious and telling him to go away: I'd come to see Linton, not him. He went red—I could see it in the moonlight—let go of the latch, and slunk away, the very picture of wounded vanity. I suppose he thought knowing how to spell his own name made him as accomplished as Linton, and he was terribly put out when I didn't agree.”

“Stop there, dear Miss Catherine!” I interrupted. “I won't scold you, but I don't like the way you behaved. If you'd remembered that Hareton is just as much your cousin as Master Heathcliff, you'd have realised how wrong it was. His wish to be as accomplished as Linton was at least something to admire. And he probably hadn't learnt just to show off. I've no doubt you'd already made him ashamed of his ignorance, and he wanted to improve himself and please you. Mocking his imperfect attempt was very ill-mannered. If _you_ had grown up as he did, would your manners be any better? As a child he was every bit as quick and intelligent as you, and it hurts me to see him despised now because that vile Heathcliff has treated him so unjustly.”

“Well, Ellen, you aren't going to cry over it, are you?” she exclaimed, surprised at how seriously I spoke. “But wait until you hear whether he learnt his ABC to please me, and whether the brute deserved any politeness. I went inside. Linton was lying on the settle and half rose to greet me.

“‘I'm ill tonight, Catherine, my love,’ he said. ‘You'll have to do all the talking and let me listen. Come and sit beside me. I knew you'd keep your promise, and I'll make you promise again before you leave.’

“Now I knew I mustn't tease him, because he was ill. I spoke gently, asked no questions, and took care not to irritate him at all. I'd brought some of my nicest books. He asked me to read a little from one, and I was just going to when Earnshaw burst through the door. Thinking things over had only made him angrier. He came straight up to us, grabbed Linton's arm, and swung him off the seat.
“‘Get to thy own room!’ he said, barely able to speak for rage, his face swollen and furious. ‘Take her there if she's come to see thee. Thou's not keeping me out of here. Off with ye, both of ye!’

“He swore at us and gave Linton no chance to answer, almost flinging him into the kitchen. As I followed he clenched his fist, looking as though he longed to knock me down. For a moment I was frightened and dropped one of the books. He kicked it after me and shut us out. I heard a spiteful, crackling laugh by the fire. Turning, I saw that hateful Joseph standing there, shaking and rubbing his bony hands.

“‘I knew he'd give ye what for! He's a grand lad! He's got t' right spirit in him! _He_ knows—aye, he knows as well as I do who ought to be t' master in there. Ech, ech, ech! He shifted ye sharp enough! Ech, ech, ech!’
“‘Where shall we go?’ I asked my cousin, ignoring the old wretch's jeering.

“Linton was pale and trembling. He wasn't pretty then, Ellen—oh, no! He looked dreadful. His thin face and large eyes were twisted with frantic, helpless fury. He seized the door handle and shook it, but the door was locked from inside.
“‘Let me in or I'll kill you! Let me in or I'll kill you!’ he screamed, rather than spoke. ‘Devil! Devil! I'll kill you—I'll kill you!’
“Joseph gave another croaking laugh.
“‘There, that's his father!’ he cried. ‘That's his father! We've always summat from each side in us. Never mind, Hareton, lad—don't thee be frightened. He can't get at thee!’

“I caught Linton's hands and tried to pull him away, but he screamed so terribly that I dared not go on. At last a dreadful coughing fit choked off his cries. Blood poured from his mouth, and he fell to the floor. Sick with terror, I ran into the yard and shouted for Zillah as loudly as I could. She soon heard me. She was milking the cows in a shed behind the barn and came hurrying to ask what was wrong. I couldn't catch my breath to explain. I dragged her inside and looked around for Linton. Earnshaw had come out to see what harm he'd done, and was carrying the poor boy upstairs. Zillah and I followed, but at the top of the stairs he stopped me and said I couldn't go in: I must go home. I cried out that he'd killed Linton and that I _would_ go in. Joseph locked the door and said I'd do ‘nowt of t' sort,’ and asked whether I was ‘going to be as mad as him.’ I stood there crying until the housekeeper came back. She said he'd be better in a little while, but couldn't bear all that shrieking and noise. Then she took hold of me and almost carried me downstairs into the main room.

“Ellen, I could have torn my hair out! I sobbed and cried until I could hardly see. And the ruffian you feel so sorry for stood opposite me, taking it upon himself every now and then to tell me to ‘hush,’ and saying it wasn't his fault. Finally my threats to tell papa and have him put in prison and hanged frightened him into blubbering too. He hurried out to hide his cowardly distress. But even then I hadn't seen the last of him. When at last they made me leave and I was a few hundred yards from the house, he suddenly stepped out of the shadows beside the road, stopped Minny, and caught hold of me.
“‘Miss Catherine, I'm sorely grieved,’ he began, ‘but it's rather too bad—’
“I struck him with my whip, thinking he might murder me. He let go, roaring one of his dreadful curses, and I galloped home almost out of my mind.

“I didn't say good night to you that evening, and the next day I didn't go to Wuthering Heights. I wanted to terribly, but I was in a strange, agitated state. One moment I dreaded hearing that Linton was dead; the next I shuddered at the thought of meeting Hareton. On the third day I found courage—or at least I couldn't bear the uncertainty any longer—and slipped away again. I went at five, on foot, thinking I might creep into the house and up to Linton's room without being seen. But the dogs announced me. Zillah welcomed me, said ‘the lad was getting on nicely,’ and took me into a small, neat, carpeted room. To my indescribable joy, there was Linton on a little sofa, reading one of my books. But for an entire hour he wouldn't speak to me or even look at me, Ellen. He has such a miserable temper. And what utterly astonished me was that when he finally spoke, he told the lie that _I_ had caused the trouble and Hareton wasn't to blame! I couldn't answer without losing my temper, so I got up and left. He called a faint ‘Catherine!’ after me. He hadn't expected me to react like that, but I wouldn't go back. The following day was the second time I stayed home, almost determined never to visit him again. Yet it was so wretched to go to bed and get up without hearing anything about him that my resolve vanished before I'd properly formed it. Once, making the journey _had_ seemed wrong; now staying away seemed wrong. Michael came to ask whether he should saddle Minny. I said yes, and as she carried me over the hills I felt I was doing my duty. To reach the yard I had to pass the front windows, so there was no point trying to hide my arrival.

“‘Young master's in the main room,’ Zillah said when she saw me heading for the parlour. I went in. Earnshaw was there too, but left at once. Linton was sitting half asleep in the big armchair. I walked up to the fire and began seriously, partly meaning what I said—

“‘Since you don't like me, Linton, and think I come here deliberately to hurt you—and claim that's what I do every time—this is our last visit. Let's say goodbye. Tell Mr. Heathcliff you don't want to see me, and he must stop making up lies about it.’

“‘Sit down and take off your hat, Catherine,’ he answered. ‘You're so much happier than I am that you ought to be better too. Papa talks about my faults enough, and shows enough contempt for me, to make it natural for me to doubt myself. I often wonder whether I'm just as worthless as he says. Then I feel so angry and bitter that I hate everyone! I _am_ worthless, bad-tempered and mean-spirited, almost all the time. And if you choose, you _can_ say goodbye: you'll be getting rid of a nuisance. Only, Catherine, be fair to me in this one thing. Believe that if I could be as sweet, as kind, and as good as you, I would choose that as readily as being happy and healthy—more readily, even. And believe that your kindness has made me love you more deeply than I would if I deserved your love. Though I couldn't help showing you what I'm like, and still can't, I regret it and I'm sorry for it. I shall regret it and be sorry until I die!’

“I felt he was telling the truth, and that I had to forgive him. Even if we quarrelled the next minute, I'd have to forgive him again. We made peace, but we both cried the whole time I stayed. It wasn't entirely from sadness, though I _was_ sad that Linton's nature was so twisted. He'll never let his friends be comfortable, and he'll never be comfortable himself! Since that evening I've always gone to his little parlour, because his father came back the day afterwards.

“About three times, I think, we've been as happy and hopeful as we were that first evening. All my other visits have been gloomy and troubled, sometimes by his selfishness and spite, sometimes by his suffering. But I've learnt to bear the first almost as patiently as the second. Mr. Heathcliff keeps out of my way on purpose; I've hardly seen him. Last Sunday, though, I arrived earlier than usual and heard him cruelly abusing poor Linton for how he'd behaved the evening before. I don't know how he knew about it, unless he'd been listening. Linton certainly had been provoking, but that was nobody's business except mine. I interrupted Mr. Heathcliff's lecture by walking in and telling him so. He burst out laughing and went away, saying he was glad I saw it that way. Since then I've told Linton he must whisper his bitter remarks. Now, Ellen, you've heard everything. You can't stop me going to Wuthering Heights without making two people miserable. But if you just don't tell papa, my visits needn't disturb anyone's peace. You won't tell him, will you? It would be very heartless if you did.”
“I'll decide that by tomorrow, Miss Catherine,” I replied. “It needs some thought, so I'll leave you to rest and go and consider it.”

I considered it aloud in my master's presence, going straight from her room to his and telling him the whole story, except for her conversations with her cousin and anything about Hareton. Mr. Linton was more alarmed and distressed than he would admit to me. In the morning Catherine discovered that I had betrayed her confidence, and that her secret visits were forbidden. She wept and struggled against the ban, begging her father to pity Linton, but it was no use. Her only consolation was his promise to write to Linton and invite him to the Grange whenever he pleased, while explaining that he could no longer expect Catherine to visit Wuthering Heights. Had he known his nephew's character and state of health, perhaps he would have thought it better to deny even that small comfort.

chapters.title: Chapter XXV
paragraphs: “All this happened last winter, sir,” said Mrs. Dean, “scarcely more than a year ago. Last winter I never imagined that twelve months later I'd be entertaining a stranger to the family by telling him about it! Still, who knows how long you'll remain a stranger? You're too young to be content with living alone for ever, and somehow I don't think anyone could see Catherine Linton without loving her. You smile—but why do you look so animated and interested whenever I talk about her? Why have you asked me to put her portrait above your fireplace? And why—?”

“Enough, my good friend!” I cried. “It's quite possible that _I_ could love her, but would she love me? I'm too doubtful of that to risk my peace of mind by exposing myself to temptation. Besides, this isn't my home. I belong to the busy world, and I must return to its embrace. Go on. Did Catherine obey her father?”

“She did,” the housekeeper continued. “Her love for him was still the strongest feeling in her heart. And he spoke without anger, with the deep tenderness of someone about to leave his greatest treasure among dangers and enemies, knowing that the memory of his words would be the only help he could leave to guide her. A few days later he said to me, ‘I wish my nephew would write, Ellen, or come to visit. Tell me honestly what you think of him. Has he improved, or is there any hope that he will as he grows into a man?’

“‘He's very frail, sir,’ I replied, ‘and hardly likely to live to manhood. But I can say this: he isn't like his father. If Miss Catherine were unfortunate enough to marry him, she could manage him, unless she foolishly indulged him far too much. Still, master, you'll have plenty of time to get to know him and decide whether he would suit her. He won't come of age for another four years or more.’”

Edgar sighed and went to the window, looking out towards Gimmerton church. The afternoon was misty, but the February sun shone faintly, and we could just make out the two fir trees in the churchyard and the scattered gravestones.

“I've often prayed,” he said, almost to himself, “for what's approaching now. And now I begin to shrink from it and feel afraid. I thought the memory of coming down that valley as a bridegroom would be less sweet than the thought of being carried back up it in a few months, perhaps only weeks, and laid in its lonely hollow! Ellen, I've been very happy with my little Cathy. Through winter nights and summer days, she has been a living hope beside me. Yet I've been just as happy thinking alone among those stones beneath the old church, lying through the long June evenings on the green mound of her mother's grave, wishing—aching—for the time when I could lie underneath it. What can I do for Cathy? How can I leave her? I wouldn't care for a moment that Linton was Heathcliff's son, or that he took her away from me, if he could comfort her when she lost me. I wouldn't care if Heathcliff got what he wanted and triumphed in robbing me of my last blessing! But if Linton is unworthy—if he's only his father's feeble tool—I can't abandon her to him. However hard it is to crush her happy spirit, I must go on making her sad while I live and leave her alone when I die. My darling! I'd rather give her up to God and lay her in the earth before me.”

“Entrust her to God now, sir,” I answered. “And if we should lose you—God forbid it—with His help I'll remain her friend and adviser to the end. Miss Catherine is a good girl. I'm not afraid she'll knowingly do wrong, and people who do their duty are always rewarded in the end.”

Spring moved on, but my master gained no real strength, though he began walking in the grounds with his daughter again. In her inexperience, she took this alone as proof that he was recovering. His cheeks were often flushed too, and his eyes bright, so she felt certain he would get well. On her seventeenth birthday he did not go to the churchyard. It was raining, and I said—
“Surely you won't go out tonight, sir?”
“No,” he answered. “This year I'll put it off a little longer.”

He wrote to Linton again, saying how much he wished to see him. Had the sick boy been fit to be seen, I have no doubt his father would have let him come. As it was, Linton replied as he had been instructed: Mr. Heathcliff objected to his visiting the Grange, but his uncle's kind concern delighted him. He hoped they might sometimes meet on his uncle's walks, when he could ask him in person not to keep him and his cousin so completely apart much longer.
That part of the letter was straightforward and probably his own. Heathcliff knew that by now he could plead eloquently for Catherine's company.

“I'm not asking,” he wrote, “for her to visit me here. But am I never to see her, because my father won't let me go to her home and you won't let her come to mine? Please ride with her towards the Heights now and then, and let us talk for a few minutes in front of you! We've done nothing to deserve being separated, and you're not angry with me. You admit yourself that you have no reason to dislike me. Dear uncle, send me a kind note tomorrow, and permission to meet you anywhere you choose except Thrushcross Grange. I believe that if we met, you'd be convinced that I don't have my father's character. He says I'm more your nephew than his son. Though I have faults that make me unworthy of Catherine, she has forgiven them, and for her sake you should too. You ask about my health. It has improved, but how can I be cheerful and well when I have no hope, and am condemned to be alone or with people who have never liked me and never will?”

Edgar felt sorry for the boy, but could not agree, since he could not accompany Catherine. Perhaps they might meet in summer, he said. Meanwhile he wanted Linton to keep writing occasionally, and promised to offer whatever advice and comfort he could by letter, knowing how hard the boy's position in his family was. Linton did as he asked. Left to himself, he would probably have ruined everything by filling his letters with complaints and lamentations. But his father watched him closely, and of course insisted on seeing every line my master sent. So instead of writing about his own particular sufferings and troubles—the things always uppermost in his mind—he kept returning to the cruelty of being forced apart from his friend and love. He gently suggested that Mr. Linton must soon let them meet, or he would begin to fear that his uncle was deliberately deceiving him with empty promises.

At home Cathy was a powerful ally. Between them they eventually persuaded my master to allow them a ride or a walk together about once a week, under my supervision, on the moors closest to the Grange. By June his health was still declining. Although he had set aside part of his income each year for my young mistress's inheritance, he naturally wanted her to keep her ancestral home—or at least return to it before long. He thought her only chance of doing so was to marry his heir. He had no idea that the boy was deteriorating almost as fast as he was himself, and I believe no one else knew either. No doctor visited the Heights, and none of us saw young Master Heathcliff to bring back news of his condition. For my part, I began to think my fears had been mistaken and that he really must be recovering, since he spoke of riding and walking on the moors and seemed so intent on getting what he wanted. I could not imagine a father treating a dying child with the tyranny and wickedness that, as I later learnt, Heathcliff used to force this apparent eagerness out of him. The more immediately death threatened to defeat his greedy, heartless plans, the harder he drove the boy.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVI
paragraphs: Summer was already past its height when Edgar reluctantly gave in to their pleas, and Catherine and I set out on our first ride to meet her cousin. The day was close and sultry, without sunshine, though the sky was too hazy and mottled to promise rain. We had agreed to meet at the guidepost by the crossroads. But when we arrived, a little herd-boy sent to meet us said, “Master Linton's just this side o' t' Heights, and he'd be much obliged if ye'd come a bit further.”
“Then Master Linton has forgotten his uncle's very first instruction,” I said. “He told us to stay on Grange land, and we're leaving it already.”
“Well, once we reach him we'll turn the horses towards home,” my companion answered. “That's the direction we'll take for our ride.”

But when we found him, scarcely a quarter of a mile from his own door, he had no horse. We had to dismount and let ours graze. He was lying on the heather waiting for us, and did not get up until we were only a few yards away. His steps were so weak and his face so pale that I exclaimed at once, “Why, Master Heathcliff, you're in no state to enjoy a walk this morning. How ill you look!”

Catherine looked at him in sorrow and astonishment. The joyful greeting on her lips became a cry of alarm, and instead of celebrating their long-delayed meeting she anxiously asked whether he was worse than usual.

“No—better—better!” he gasped, trembling and holding on to her hand as though he needed it to support him. His large blue eyes moved timidly over her. The hollows around them had changed their once languid expression into something haggard and wild.
“But you have been worse,” his cousin insisted. “Worse than when I last saw you. You're thinner, and—”
“I'm tired,” he interrupted quickly. “It's too hot to walk. Let's rest here. And I often feel sick in the mornings. Papa says it's because I'm growing so fast.”
Far from reassured, Cathy sat down, and he lay beside her.

“This is rather like your paradise,” she said, trying to sound cheerful. “Do you remember the two days we agreed to spend in the places and ways each of us liked best? This is almost your day, except for the clouds. But they're so soft and gentle that it's nicer than sunshine. Next week, if you're able, we'll ride down to the Grange park and try mine.”

Linton did not seem to remember what she meant, and clearly found any sort of conversation a great effort. His indifference to the subjects she raised, and his complete inability to offer anything to entertain her, were so obvious that she could not hide her disappointment. Some indefinable change had come over his whole appearance and manner. The petulance that affection could turn to tenderness had given way to listless apathy. He seemed less like an irritable child who frets and teases to be comforted, and more like a chronic invalid, sullenly absorbed in himself, rejecting comfort and ready to take anyone else's cheerful laughter as an insult. Catherine saw as clearly as I did that he found our company more of a punishment than a pleasure, and before long she freely suggested leaving. Unexpectedly, the suggestion roused him from his lethargy and made him strangely agitated. He glanced towards the Heights in fear and begged her to stay at least another half-hour.

“But I think you'd be more comfortable at home than sitting here,” Cathy said. “I can see my stories and songs and chatter aren't amusing you today. You've grown wiser than I have in these six months; you don't much care for my amusements now. If I could entertain you, I'd gladly stay.”

“Stay and rest yourself,” he replied. “And, Catherine, don't think or say I'm _very_ ill. It's the muggy weather and the heat that make me so dull. And before you came I walked about quite a lot—for me. Tell uncle I'm fairly well, will you?”
“I'll tell him _you_ say so, Linton. I couldn't tell him you are,” my young mistress said, puzzled that he kept insisting on something so plainly untrue.

“And come back here next Thursday,” he went on, avoiding her bewildered eyes. “Thank him for letting you come—thank him very much, Catherine. And—and if you _did_ happen to meet my father and he asked about me, don't let him think I've been terribly quiet and stupid. Don't look sad and downhearted the way you _are_ looking. He'll be angry.”
“I don't care if he's angry,” Cathy cried, thinking his anger would be directed at her.
“But I do,” her cousin said with a shudder. “_Don't_ turn him against me, Catherine. He's very harsh.”
“Does he treat you harshly, Master Heathcliff?” I asked. “Has he tired of indulging you and begun to act on his hatred, instead of merely feeling it?”

Linton looked at me without answering. Cathy stayed beside him another ten minutes. His head drooped sleepily onto his chest, and he made no sound except muffled groans of exhaustion or pain. Then she tried to find some consolation in gathering bilberries and sharing her finds with me. She offered him none, seeing that any further attention would only tire and annoy him.
“Has it been half an hour yet, Ellen?” she whispered in my ear at last. “I don't know why we're staying. He's asleep, and papa will want us home.”
“Well, we can't leave him sleeping,” I answered. “Be patient and wait until he wakes. You were so eager to set out, but your longing to see poor Linton has worn off quickly enough!”

“Why did _he_ want to see me?” Catherine replied. “I liked him better in his worst tempers before than I do in this strange mood. It's as though seeing us were a task he's being forced to do for fear his father will scold him. But I'm certainly not coming here to please Mr. Heathcliff, whatever reason he has for making Linton go through this punishment. And although I'm glad his health is better, I'm sorry he's so much less pleasant and so much less affectionate towards me.”
“So you think his health _has_ improved?” I said.
“Yes,” she answered. “You know how he always made so much of his suffering. He's not fairly well, as he wanted me to tell papa, but he's probably better.”
“I don't agree with you there, Miss Cathy,” I said. “I should think he's much worse.”
At that moment Linton woke with a start, bewildered and terrified, and asked whether someone had called his name.
“No,” Catherine said, “unless it was in your dreams. I don't understand how you can fall asleep outdoors in the morning.”
“I thought I heard my father,” he gasped, looking up at the dark, overhanging crag above us. “Are you sure no one spoke?”

“Quite sure,” his cousin replied. “Ellen and I were only disagreeing about your health. Are you really stronger than when we last met in winter, Linton? If you are, there's one thing I'm certain hasn't grown stronger: your affection for me. Tell me—are you?”
Tears streamed from Linton's eyes as he answered, “Yes, yes, I am!” Still gripped by the voice he had imagined, he kept looking up and down for the person it belonged to.

Cathy stood up. “We must say goodbye for today,” she said. “I won't pretend I haven't been terribly disappointed by our meeting, though I won't tell anyone but you. That's not because I'm afraid of Mr. Heathcliff.”

“Hush!” Linton murmured. “For God's sake, hush! He's coming.” He clung to Catherine's arm, trying to hold her back, but at those words she quickly pulled free and whistled to Minny, who came to her like a dog.
“I'll be here next Thursday,” she called, springing into the saddle. “Goodbye. Hurry, Ellen!”
And so we left him. He was hardly aware that we were going, so completely was he occupied by the thought of his father's approach.

Before we reached home, Catherine's annoyance had softened into a confused mixture of pity and regret, mingled with vague, uneasy doubts about Linton's real condition, both in his health and his life at home. I shared those doubts, but advised her to say little: another visit would help us judge better. My master asked how our outing had gone. We duly passed on his nephew's thanks, and Miss Cathy touched lightly on the rest. My answers gave him little more information, for I hardly knew what I should conceal and what I should reveal.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVII
paragraphs: Seven days slipped by, each bringing a further, now rapid change in Edgar Linton's condition. The damage that once took months was now being done in hours. We would gladly have kept Catherine deceived, but her own quick understanding would not let her deceive herself. In secret she guessed at the dreadful likelihood and dwelt on it as it gradually became a certainty. When Thursday came she had no heart to mention her ride. I mentioned it for her and got permission to insist on her going outdoors. Her whole world had become her father's bedroom and the library, where he spent the short time each day that he could bear to sit up. She resented every moment not spent bending over his pillow or sitting beside him. Watching and sorrow had made her pale. My master willingly sent her out for what he hoped would be a happy change of scene and company, comforting himself with the thought that after his death she would not be entirely alone.

From several remarks he let fall, I gathered he had firmly persuaded himself that, since his nephew resembled him in looks, their minds would be alike too. Linton's letters gave little or no sign of his flawed character. Out of an excusable weakness, I did not correct the mistake. What good, I asked myself, would it do to trouble his last moments with knowledge he had neither the strength nor the opportunity to act upon?

We put off our outing until the afternoon—a golden August afternoon. Every breath of air from the hills seemed so full of life that anyone who breathed it, even someone dying, might revive. Catherine's face was like the landscape: sunshine and shadow passed over it in quick succession, but the shadows stayed longer and the sunshine faded sooner. Even that brief forgetting of her troubles made her poor little heart reproach itself.

We saw Linton waiting at the same place as before. My young mistress dismounted and told me that, as she meant to stay only a very short time, I had better remain on horseback and hold her pony. I refused. I would not risk letting the girl in my care out of my sight for a minute, so we climbed the heather slope together. This time Master Heathcliff greeted us with more animation, but it was neither high spirits nor happiness. It looked more like fear.
“You're late!” he said, struggling to get the short words out. “Isn't your father very ill? I thought you wouldn't come.”

“_Why_ can't you be honest?” cried Catherine, holding back her greeting. “Why not simply say you don't want me? It's strange, Linton: this is the second time you've deliberately brought me here, apparently for no reason except to upset us both!”
Linton shuddered and looked at her, half pleading, half ashamed. But his cousin had too little patience to put up with such baffling behaviour.

“My father _is_ very ill,” she said, “so why am I being called away from his bedside? If you didn't want me to keep my promise, why didn't you send word to release me from it? Come, explain yourself! I've no thought for games or nonsense now, and I can't spend my time attending to your affectations!”

“My affectations?” he murmured. “What do you mean? For heaven's sake, Catherine, don't look so angry! Despise me as much as you like.
