I'm a worthless, cowardly wretch, and no one could despise me enough. But I'm too contemptible to deserve your anger. Hate my father; keep only your contempt for me.”

“Nonsense!” Catherine cried furiously. “You foolish, silly boy! And look at him trembling, as though I were really going to touch him! You needn't ask for contempt, Linton. Anyone will give you that without being asked. Let go! I'm going home. It's ridiculous dragging you away from the fireside and pretending—what are we pretending? Let go of my dress! If I pitied you for crying and looking so frightened, you ought to reject such pity. Ellen, tell him how shameful this is. Get up! Don't lower yourself into a grovelling reptile—_don't_!”
With tears pouring down his face and agony in his expression, Linton had flung his powerless body along the ground. He seemed to be shaking with unbearable terror.

“Oh!” he sobbed. “I can't bear it! Catherine, Catherine, I'm a traitor too, and I daren't tell you! But if you leave me, I'll be killed! _Dear_ Catherine, my life is in your hands. You've said you love me, and if you did it, it wouldn't hurt you. You won't go, then? Kind, sweet, good Catherine! Perhaps you _will_ agree—and he'll let me die with you!”
Seeing his terrible distress, my young mistress bent to lift him. Her old, indulgent tenderness overcame her irritation, and she was deeply moved and frightened.

“Agree to what?” she asked. “To stay? Tell me what this strange talk means, and I will. You keep contradicting yourself, and you're driving me distracted! Calm down, be honest, and tell me at once everything that's troubling you. You wouldn't hurt me, would you, Linton? You wouldn't let an enemy harm me if you could stop them? I can believe you'd be a coward where you're concerned, but not a coward who betrays his best friend.”
“But my father threatened me,” the boy gasped, clasping his wasted fingers. “I'm terrified of him—terrified! I _daren't_ tell!”
“Oh, very well!” Catherine said with scornful pity. “Keep your secret. _I'm_ not a coward. Save yourself. I'm not afraid!”

Her generosity brought on fresh tears. He sobbed wildly and kissed the hands supporting him, yet still could not find the courage to speak plainly. I was wondering what lay behind all this, determined that Catherine should never suffer for his benefit or anyone else's if I could help it, when I heard a rustle in the heather. Looking up, I saw Mr. Heathcliff coming down from the Heights, almost upon us. He did not glance at my companions, though they were close enough for him to hear Linton sobbing. Instead he greeted me in the almost friendly tone he used with no one else, and whose sincerity I could never quite trust.

“It's something to find you so near my house, Nelly. How are things at the Grange? Tell me. The rumour is,” he added more quietly, “that Edgar Linton is on his deathbed. Perhaps they exaggerate how ill he is?”
“No, my master is dying,” I answered. “That's true enough. It will be a sad thing for us all, but a blessing for him!”
“How long do you think he'll last?” he asked.
“I don't know,” I replied.

“Because,” he continued, looking at the two young people, who froze under his gaze—Linton seemed afraid even to move or lift his head, and Catherine could not move because of him—“because that boy there seems determined to defeat me, and I'd be obliged if his uncle would hurry up and go first! Hallo! Has the whelp been at that game long? I _did_ teach him a thing or two about snivelling. Is he usually fairly lively with Miss Linton?”
“Lively? No. He's been terribly distressed,” I answered. “Judging by his appearance, he ought to be in bed with a doctor attending him, instead of walking on the hills with his sweetheart.”
“He will be, in a day or two,” Heathcliff muttered. “But first—get up, Linton! Get up!” he shouted. “Stop grovelling on the ground. Up, this instant!”

Linton had collapsed again in another fit of helpless terror, brought on, I suppose, by his father's glance: nothing else could account for such abasement. He tried several times to obey, but for the moment his little strength had entirely deserted him, and he fell back with a groan. Mr. Heathcliff stepped forward and lifted him to lean against a ridge of turf.
“Now,” he said with barely restrained savagery, “I'm getting angry. And if you don't control that miserable spirit of yours—_damn_ you! Get up at once!”

“I will, father,” he panted. “Only leave me alone, or I'll faint. I'm sure I've done what you wanted. Catherine will tell you I've—that I've—been cheerful. Oh, stay beside me, Catherine! Give me your hand.”

“Take mine,” his father said. “Stand on your feet. There—she'll give you her arm. That's right, look at _her_. You'd think I was the devil himself, Miss Linton, to inspire such terror. Would you be so kind as to walk home with him? He shudders when I touch him.”
“Dear Linton,” Catherine whispered, “I can't go to Wuthering Heights. Papa has forbidden it. He won't hurt you. Why are you so frightened?”
“I can never go back into that house,” he answered. “I'm _not allowed_ to go back without you!”
“Enough!” his father cried. “We'll respect Catherine's scruples about obeying her father. Nelly, take him inside, and I'll follow your advice about a doctor at once.”
“That would be wise,” I replied. “But I must stay with my mistress. Looking after your son isn't my business.”

“You're very stubborn, I know,” said Heathcliff. “But you'll make me pinch the baby and set it screaming before I can stir your charity. Come along, then, my hero. Will you go home with me escorting you?”

He came towards him again as if to seize the frail creature. Linton shrank back and clung to his cousin, begging her to go with him with such frantic insistence that refusal was impossible. However much I disapproved, I could not stop her. Indeed, how could she herself have refused? We had no way of knowing what frightened him, but it held him helpless, and any further shock seemed enough to rob him of his wits. We reached the doorway. Catherine went in, and I waited while she helped the invalid to a chair, expecting her to return at once. Then Mr. Heathcliff pushed me forward, exclaiming, “My house hasn't got the plague, Nelly. And I'm feeling hospitable today. Sit down and let me shut the door.”
He not only shut it, but locked it. I started in alarm.

“You'll have tea before you go home,” he added. “I'm alone. Hareton has taken some cattle to the Lees, and Zillah and Joseph are away enjoying themselves. Though I'm used to solitude, I'd rather have interesting company when I can get it. Miss Linton, sit beside _him_. I give you what I've got. It's a present hardly worth accepting, but I have nothing else to offer. I mean Linton. How she stares! It's strange how savage I feel towards anything that seems frightened of me. If I'd been born somewhere with fewer laws and less delicate tastes, I'd amuse myself of an evening by slowly cutting those two open alive.”
He drew a breath, struck the table, and swore to himself, “By hell! I hate them.”

“I'm not afraid of you!” Catherine exclaimed. She had not heard the last part of his speech. She stepped right up to him, her dark eyes flashing with anger and determination. “Give me that key. I _will_ have it!” she said. “I wouldn't eat or drink in this house if I were starving.”

The key lay in Heathcliff's hand, which still rested on the table. He looked up, apparently surprised by her boldness—or perhaps her voice and look reminded him of the person from whom she had inherited it. She snatched at the key and almost pulled it from his slackened fingers. But her movement brought him back to the present, and he quickly recovered it.
“Now, Catherine Linton,” he said, “stand back, or I'll knock you down. And that will make Mrs. Dean furious.”

Ignoring the warning, she caught his closed hand and the key again. “We _will_ leave!” she repeated, struggling with all her strength to force those iron muscles to loosen. When her nails made no impression, she bit him sharply. Heathcliff shot me a look that stopped me intervening for a moment. Catherine was too intent on his fingers to notice his face. Suddenly he opened his hand and let her have the disputed object. But before she had a firm hold of it, he seized her with his freed hand and pulled her onto his knee. With the other hand he rained terrible blows on both sides of her head, any one of which would have fulfilled his threat if she had been free to fall.

At this fiendish violence I rushed at him in a fury. “You villain!” I began shouting. “You villain!” A push against my chest silenced me. I am stout and easily winded, and between that and my rage I staggered back dizzily, feeling as though I would suffocate or burst a blood vessel. It was all over in two minutes. Released, Catherine put both hands to her temples and looked as though she could not tell whether her ears were still attached. The poor girl shook like a reed and leaned against the table, utterly dazed.

“You see, I know how to discipline children,” the scoundrel said grimly, stooping to retrieve the key from the floor. “Now go to Linton as I told you, and cry as much as you please! Tomorrow I'll be your father—all the father you'll have in a few days—and you'll get plenty of that. You can take plenty; you're no weakling. You'll have a taste of it every day if I catch that devilish temper in your eyes again!”

Instead of going to Linton, Cathy ran to me, knelt down, and laid her burning cheek in my lap, sobbing aloud. Her cousin had shrunk into a corner of the settle, quiet as a mouse, no doubt congratulating himself that someone else had received the punishment. Seeing us all overwhelmed, Mr. Heathcliff stood up and briskly made the tea himself. The cups and saucers were already laid out. He poured the tea and handed me a cup.
“Wash down your anger,” he said. “And give some to your naughty pet and mine. It's not poisoned, though I made it. I'm going to find your horses.”
As soon as he left, our first thought was to force a way out. We tried the kitchen door, but it was fastened from outside. We examined the windows: they were too narrow even for Cathy's small figure.
“Master Linton,” I cried, realising we were truly imprisoned, “you know what that devil of a father of yours is planning, and you'll tell us, or I'll box your ears as he boxed your cousin's.”
“Yes, Linton, you must tell us,” Catherine said. “I came for your sake. Refusing would be wickedly ungrateful.”

“Give me some tea—I'm thirsty—and then I'll tell you,” he answered. “Mrs. Dean, move away. I don't like you standing over me. Now, Catherine, you're crying into my cup. I won't drink that. Give me another.”

Catherine pushed another cup towards him and wiped her face. The little wretch's calmness, now that he no longer feared for himself, disgusted me. His distress on the moor had vanished the moment he entered Wuthering Heights. I guessed he had been threatened with a terrible outburst of fury if he failed to lure us there, and now that he had succeeded he had nothing more to fear for the moment.

“Papa wants us to get married,” he continued after taking a sip. “He knows your papa wouldn't let us marry now, and he's afraid I'll die if we wait. So we're to marry tomorrow morning, and you must stay here all night. If you do what he wants, you can go home the day after and take me with you.”

“Take you with her, you pitiful changeling!” I exclaimed. “_You_, marry? The man's mad, or he thinks we're all fools. Do you imagine that beautiful young lady, that healthy, lively girl, will tie herself to a little dying monkey like you? Do you really believe _anyone_, let alone Miss Catherine Linton, would have you for a husband? You deserve a whipping for bringing us here at all with your cowardly, whining tricks. And don't look so stupid now! I've a very good mind to give you a thorough shaking for your contemptible treachery and your idiotic conceit.”
I did shake him a little, but it started his cough, and he fell back on his usual defence of groaning and crying. Catherine reproached me.
“Stay all night? No,” she said, slowly looking around. “Ellen, I'll burn that door down if that's what it takes to get out.”

She would have carried out her threat at once, but Linton sprang up, terrified for his precious self again. He clasped her in his two weak arms and sobbed, “Won't you marry me and save me? Won't you let me come to the Grange? Oh, darling Catherine, you mustn't leave me after all! You _must_ obey my father—you _must_!”

“I must obey my own,” she replied, “and put an end to this cruel uncertainty for him. The whole night! What would he think? He'll be worried already. I'll break my way out of this house or burn my way out. Be quiet! You're in no danger. But if you stop me—Linton, I love papa more than you!”

His mortal fear of Mr. Heathcliff's anger restored the boy's cowardly eloquence. Catherine was almost beside herself, but still insisted she must go home. Now she tried pleading too, urging him to master his selfish distress. While they were occupied in this way, our jailer came back.

“Your animals have trotted off,” he said. “And—now, Linton! Snivelling again? What's she been doing to you? Come, come, stop it and go to bed. In a month or two, my boy, you'll have a strong enough hand to repay her for bullying you now. You're wasting away from love alone, aren't you? Nothing else in the world. And she shall have you! Now, to bed. Zillah won't be here tonight; you'll have to undress yourself. Hush! Stop that noise! Once you're in your own room, I won't come near you. You needn't be frightened. You've managed tolerably well, by chance. I'll deal with the rest.”

As he spoke, he held the door open for his son. Linton slipped past exactly like a spaniel suspecting that the person attending to it meant to give it a spiteful squeeze. The door was locked again. Heathcliff came over to the fire, where my mistress and I stood silently. Catherine looked up and instinctively raised a hand to her cheek: his nearness had revived the pain. Anyone else would have been softened by that childish gesture, but he scowled at her and muttered, “Oh, so you're not afraid of me? You hide your courage well. You _seem_ damnably frightened!”

“I _am_ frightened now,” she replied, “because if I stay, papa will be miserable. And how can I bear to make him miserable when he—when he—Mr. Heathcliff, _let_ me go home! I promise I'll marry Linton. Papa would like me to, and I love him. Why force me to do something I'd willingly do myself?”

“Let him try to force you!” I cried. “Thank God there's law in this country, even in a place as remote as this! I'd report him if he were my own son. It's a felony, with no benefit of clergy to save him!”

“Silence!” the ruffian said. “To hell with your shouting! I don't want _you_ speaking. Miss Linton, the thought of your father's misery will give me immense pleasure. I shall be too satisfied to sleep. You couldn't have found a surer way of keeping yourself under my roof for the next twenty-four hours than telling me that would be the result. As for your promise to marry Linton, I'll see that you keep it. You won't leave here until you have.”
“Then send Ellen to tell papa I'm safe!” Catherine cried, weeping bitterly. “Or marry me now. Poor papa! Ellen, he'll think we're lost. What can we do?”

“Nothing of the sort! He'll think you've grown tired of nursing him and run off for a little amusement,” Heathcliff answered. “You can't deny you came into my house of your own accord, against his express orders. And it's quite natural to want amusement at your age, and to grow tired of nursing a sick man when he's _only_ your father. Catherine, his happiest days ended when your life began. I dare say he cursed you for coming into the world—I certainly did—and it would be only fitting if he cursed you as _he_ left it. I'd join him. I don't love you! Why should I? Cry away. From what I can see, crying will be your chief amusement from now on, unless Linton makes up for your other losses. Your far-seeing parent seems to think he might. His letters of advice and comfort entertained me enormously. In the last one he told my jewel to take care of his, and to be kind to her once he had her. Careful and kind—how fatherly! But Linton needs all his care and kindness for himself. He makes an excellent little tyrant. He'll torture any number of cats, provided their teeth have been pulled and their claws cut. You'll have fine stories of his _kindness_ for his uncle when you get home, I assure you.”
“Quite right!” I said. “Explain your son's character. Show her how like you he is. Then I hope Miss Cathy will think twice before she takes that cockatrice!”

“I don't much mind discussing his charming qualities now,” he answered. “She must either accept him or stay a prisoner, with you beside her, until your master dies. I can keep you both here completely hidden. If you doubt it, encourage her to break her promise. Then you'll have a chance to find out!”

“I won't break my promise,” Catherine said. “I'll marry him within the hour if I can go to Thrushcross Grange afterwards. Mr. Heathcliff, you're cruel, but you're not a fiend. You won't destroy all my happiness for ever out of _pure_ malice. If papa thought I'd left him deliberately, and died before I got back, how could I bear to live? I've stopped crying. But I'm going to kneel here beside your knee, and I won't get up or take my eyes off your face until you look back at me! No, don't turn away. _Do_ look! You won't see anything to anger you. I don't hate you. I'm not angry that you hit me. Have you never loved _anyone_ in your whole life, uncle? _Never_? Ah, you must look at me once. I'm so miserable, you can't help feeling sorry for me and pitying me.”

“Keep your lizard fingers off me! Move, or I'll kick you!” Heathcliff cried, roughly thrusting her away. “I'd rather be embraced by a snake. How the devil can you think of fawning on me? I _detest_ you!”

He shrugged, then actually shook himself as though disgust made his flesh crawl, and pushed back his chair. I stood up and opened my mouth to unleash a torrent of abuse. But he silenced me halfway through my first sentence by threatening to put me in a room alone if I uttered another syllable. It was getting dark. We heard voices at the garden gate. Our host hurried out at once. _He_ had kept his wits; _we_ had not. After two or three minutes of conversation, he came back alone.
“I thought that was your cousin Hareton,” I said to Catherine. “I wish he'd come! Who knows—he might take our side.”

“It was three servants from the Grange, sent to look for you,” Heathcliff said, overhearing me. “You should have opened a window and called out. But I'd swear the little minx is glad you didn't. I'm certain she's pleased to be forced to stay.”

When we learnt what chance we had missed, we both gave way to uncontrollable grief. He let us cry until nine, then ordered us upstairs through the kitchen to Zillah's room. I whispered to my companion to obey: perhaps we could get through the window there, or into an attic and out through its skylight. But the window was as narrow as those downstairs, and the attic trapdoor was beyond our reach, for we were locked in as before. Neither of us lay down. Catherine stood by the window, anxiously watching for morning. My repeated pleas that she try to rest brought only a deep sigh. I sat in a chair rocking backwards and forwards, bitterly condemning the many times I had failed in my duty. It seemed to me then that all my employers' misfortunes had sprung from those failures. I know that was not really true, but on that wretched night I imagined it was, and thought even Heathcliff less guilty than myself.

At seven he came and asked whether Miss Linton was up. She ran straight to the door and answered yes. “Come, then,” he said, opening it and pulling her out. I got up to follow, but he locked it again. I demanded to be let out.
“Be patient,” he replied. “I'll send your breakfast up in a little while.”

I hammered on the panels and angrily rattled the latch. Catherine asked why I was still locked in. He said I must try to bear it for another hour, and they went away. I bore it for two or three hours. At last I heard footsteps, which were not Heathcliff's.
“I've brought ye something to eat,” a voice said. “Open t' door!”
I hurried to obey and found Hareton carrying enough food to last me the day.
“Take it,” he added, thrusting the tray into my hands.
“Wait a moment,” I began.
“Nay,” he cried, and left, paying no attention to any plea I could make to hold him there.

I remained locked up all that day, all the following night, and then another, and another. Altogether I spent five nights and four days there, seeing nobody but Hareton once each morning. He was a perfect jailer: surly and silent, deaf to every attempt to appeal to his justice or compassion.

chapters.title: Chapter XXVIII
paragraphs: On the fifth morning—or rather, afternoon—I heard a different step approaching, lighter and shorter. This time the visitor came into the room. It was Zillah, wearing her scarlet shawl and a black silk bonnet, with a wicker basket on her arm.

“Dear me, Mrs. Dean!” she exclaimed. “Well, they're talking about you in Gimmerton! I thought you'd sunk in the Blackhorse marsh, with missy beside you, until the master told me you'd been found and he was keeping you here! You must have got onto an island, surely? How long were you stuck in that hole? Did the master save you, Mrs. Dean? But you haven't grown so thin. You haven't been that poorly, have you?”
“Your master is a thorough scoundrel!” I answered. “But he'll answer for it. He needn't have made up that story. I'll expose the whole thing!”

“What do you mean?” Zillah asked. “It's not his story. That's what they're saying in the village—that you were lost in the marsh. When I came in, I called to Earnshaw, ‘Eh, Mr. Hareton, strange things have happened while I've been away. What a pity about that fine young girl and lively Nelly Dean.’ He stared. I thought he hadn't heard, so I told him the rumour. The master listened, then just smiled to himself and said, ‘If they've been in the marsh, they're out now, Zillah. Nelly Dean is staying in your room this very minute. When you go up, tell her to be off. Here's the key. The bog water went to her head, and she'd have run home quite delirious, but I kept her here until she came to her senses. Tell her to go to the Grange at once if she's able, and take a message from me: her young lady will follow in time for the squire's funeral.’”
“Mr. Edgar isn't dead?” I gasped. “Oh, Zillah, Zillah!”
“No, no. Sit down, my good woman,” she replied. “You're still quite unwell. He's not dead. Doctor Kenneth thinks he might last another day. I met him on the road and asked.”

Instead of sitting down, I snatched up my outdoor clothes and hurried downstairs, since the way was open. In the main room I looked for someone who could tell me about Catherine. Sunlight filled the room, and the door stood wide open, but no one seemed to be there. I hesitated between leaving at once and going back to look for my mistress. Then a faint cough drew my attention to the hearth. Linton was lying alone on the settle, sucking a stick of sugar candy and following my movements with indifferent eyes. “Where is Miss Catherine?” I demanded sternly, thinking that, now I had caught him alone, I could frighten him into answering. He went on sucking his sweet as innocently as ever.
“Has she gone?” I asked.
“No,” he answered. “She's upstairs. She's not allowed to go. We won't let her.”
“You won't let her, you little idiot!” I exclaimed. “Tell me where her room is this minute, or I'll make you cry out.”

“Papa would make _you_ cry out if you tried to go there,” he replied. “He says I mustn't be soft with Catherine. She's my wife, and it's disgraceful of her to want to leave me. He says she hates me and wants me to die so she can have my money. But she shan't have it, and she shan't go home! Never! She can cry and be ill as much as she likes!”
He went back to his sweet, closing his eyes as though he intended to fall asleep.

“Master Heathcliff,” I began again, “have you forgotten all Catherine's kindness last winter, when you said you loved her? She brought you books and sang to you, and came again and again through wind and snow to see you. She cried if she missed one evening because you'd be disappointed. You felt then that she was a hundred times too good to you. And now you believe your father's lies, though you know he hates you both. You take his side against her. What fine gratitude!”
The corner of Linton's mouth drooped, and he took the sugar candy away from his lips.

“Did she come to Wuthering Heights because she hated you?” I went on. “Think for yourself! As for your money, she doesn't even know you'll have any. You say she's ill, yet you leave her alone upstairs in a strange house! _You_, who know what it means to be neglected like that! You could pity your own suffering, and she pitied it too, but you won't pity hers. Look, Master Heathcliff, I'm crying—an older woman, and only a servant. Yet you, after pretending to love her so much, and with almost every reason to worship her, save all your tears for yourself and lie there quite comfortably. Oh, you're a heartless, selfish boy!”

“I can't stay with her,” he answered crossly. “And I won't stay on my own. She cries so much I can't bear it. She won't stop even when I tell her I'll call my father. I did call him once, and he threatened to strangle her if she wasn't quiet. But the moment he left she started again, groaning and grieving all night, though I screamed with annoyance because I couldn't sleep.”
“Is Mr. Heathcliff out?” I asked, seeing that the miserable creature was incapable of feeling for his cousin's mental agony.

“He's in the yard,” he replied, “talking to Doctor Kenneth, who says uncle really is dying at last. I'm glad: I'll be master of the Grange after him. Catherine always called it _her_ house. It isn't hers! It's mine. Papa says everything she has belongs to me. All her lovely books are mine. She offered them to me, and her pretty birds and her pony Minny, if I'd get our room key and let her out. But I told her she had nothing to give: it was all, all mine. Then she cried and took a little picture from around her neck and said I could have that. There were two pictures in a gold case, her mother on one side and uncle on the other, when they were young. That was yesterday. I said _those_ were mine too, and tried to take them. The spiteful thing wouldn't let me. She pushed me away and hurt me. I screamed—that frightens her. She heard papa coming, broke the hinges to separate the case, and gave me her mother's picture. She tried to hide the other one, but papa asked what was wrong, and I told him. He took my picture away and ordered her to give me hers. She refused, and he—he knocked her down, tore it off the chain, and crushed it under his foot.”
“Did it please you to see her hit?” I asked. I had a purpose in encouraging him to talk.

“I flinched,” he answered. “I flinch when my father hits a dog or a horse, he hits so hard. But I was glad at first. She deserved punishment for pushing me. After papa went, though, she made me come to the window and showed me where her teeth had cut the inside of her cheek and how her mouth was filling with blood. Then she picked up the pieces of the picture and sat down facing the wall. She hasn't spoken to me since. Sometimes I think she's in too much pain to speak. I don't like thinking that, but she's naughty to keep crying. And she looks so pale and wild that I'm afraid of her.”
“So you can get the key if you want to?” I said.
“Yes, when I'm upstairs,” he answered. “But I can't walk up there now.”
“Which room is it in?” I asked.

“Oh, I'm not telling _you_ where it is!” he cried. “That's our secret. Nobody's to know, not Hareton or Zillah. There, you've tired me out. Go away, go away!” He turned his face onto his arm and closed his eyes again.

I decided it would be best to leave without seeing Mr. Heathcliff and bring help from the Grange to rescue my young mistress. When I arrived there, my fellow servants were overwhelmed with surprise and joy. On hearing that their little mistress was safe, two or three were ready to rush upstairs and shout the news through Mr. Edgar's door, but I insisted on telling him myself. How much he had changed, even in those few days! He lay awaiting death, the picture of sadness and resignation. He looked very young. He was thirty-nine, but anyone would have taken him for at least ten years younger. His thoughts were on Catherine, for he murmured her name. I touched his hand and spoke.
“Catherine is coming, dear master,” I whispered. “She's alive and well. I hope she'll be here tonight.”

His first response to the news frightened me. He half sat up, looked eagerly around the room, then sank back unconscious. Once he recovered, I told him about our forced visit and imprisonment at the Heights. I said Heathcliff had made me go inside, which was not quite true. I spoke as little as possible against Linton and did not describe all his father's brutality. If I could help it, I meant to add no further bitterness to a cup already overflowing.

He understood that one of his enemy's aims was to secure the personal fortune as well as the estate for his son—or rather, for himself. But my master could not understand why he had not waited for his death, being unaware how close together he and his nephew would leave the world. Still, he thought it best to change his will. Instead of leaving Catherine free to dispose of her fortune, he decided to place it in the hands of trustees for her use during her lifetime, and afterwards for any children she might have. That way it could not pass to Mr. Heathcliff if Linton died.

On his orders, I sent one man for the lawyer and four others, equipped with useful weapons, to demand my young mistress from her jailer. Both parties were delayed until very late. The servant sent alone returned first. Mr. Green, the lawyer, had been out, he said, and he had waited two hours for him. Then Mr. Green said he had a little business in the village that must be attended to, but would be at Thrushcross Grange before morning. The other four men also returned without her. Catherine was ill, they reported, too ill to leave her room, and Heathcliff would not let them see her. I gave the fools a thorough scolding for believing that tale and refused to repeat it to my master. At daylight, I resolved, I would take a whole crowd to the Heights and literally storm the house unless they handed over their prisoner peacefully. Her father _would_ see her, I swore again and again, even if that devil had to be killed on his own doorstep for trying to stop it!

Fortunately, I was spared both the journey and the struggle. At three o'clock I had gone downstairs for a jug of water and was carrying it through the hall when a sharp knock at the front door startled me. “Oh, it's Green,” I said, recovering myself. “Only Green.” I walked on, meaning to send someone else to let him in, but the knock came again, not loudly, yet insistently. I set the jug on the banister and hurried to the door myself. Outside, the harvest moon shone clearly. It was not the lawyer. My own dear little mistress flung her arms around my neck, sobbing, “Ellen, Ellen! Is papa alive?”
“Yes!” I cried. “Yes, my angel, he is! Thank God you're safely back with us!”

Breathless as she was, she wanted to run upstairs to Mr. Linton's room. I made her sit down instead, gave her something to drink, and washed her pale face, rubbing it with my apron until a little colour returned. Then I told her I must go first to announce her arrival. I begged her to say she would be happy with young Heathcliff. She stared at me, but soon understood why I was urging her to tell that lie, and promised she would not complain.

I couldn't bear to witness their reunion. For a quarter of an hour I stood outside the bedroom door, and even then hardly dared approach the bed. But all was quiet. Catherine's despair was as silent as her father's joy. To outward appearances she supported him calmly, while he raised his eyes to her face, and they seemed to widen with rapture.

He died in perfect happiness, Mr. Lockwood. That is how he died. Kissing her cheek, he murmured, “I'm going to her, and you, darling child, will come to us!” He never moved or spoke again, but kept that radiant, absorbed gaze until his pulse stopped imperceptibly and his soul left him. No one could have marked the exact moment of his death. There was no struggle at all.

Whether Catherine had no tears left, or her grief was too heavy to let them flow, she sat there dry-eyed until sunrise. She stayed until noon and would have gone on keeping watch over that deathbed if I had not insisted she come away and rest. It was fortunate I persuaded her, for at dinner time the lawyer arrived, having first called at Wuthering Heights for instructions. He had sold himself to Mr. Heathcliff: that explained his delay in answering my master's summons. Fortunately, after his daughter's return, no thoughts of worldly business had troubled the dying man's mind.

Mr. Green assumed authority over everyone and everything in the house. He dismissed all the servants except me. He would even have stretched his borrowed powers so far as to insist that Edgar Linton be buried in the chapel with his family rather than beside his wife. But the will prevented that, along with my loud protests against any departure from its instructions. The funeral was hurried through. Catherine, now Mrs. Linton Heathcliff, was allowed to remain at the Grange until her father's body had been taken away.

She told me that her agony had finally driven Linton to risk setting her free. She had heard my men arguing at the door and understood the meaning of Heathcliff's answer. It made her desperate. Linton, who had been carried up to the little parlour soon after I left, was frightened into fetching the key before his father came upstairs again. He was cunning enough to unlock the door and turn the lock again without shutting it. When bedtime came, he asked to sleep with Hareton, and for once his request was granted. Catherine slipped out before dawn. Afraid the dogs would raise the alarm, she dared not try the doors. Instead she searched the empty rooms and examined their windows. Luckily she found her mother's room, and by the fir tree close beside it she easily climbed out of the window and down to the ground. Despite his timid precautions, her accomplice suffered for his part in the escape.

chapters.title: Chapter XXIX
paragraphs: The evening after the funeral, my young mistress and I sat in the library, sometimes dwelling sorrowfully—one of us hopelessly—on our loss, sometimes daring to speculate about the dark future ahead.

We had just agreed that the best Catherine could hope for was permission to stay at the Grange, at least while Linton lived, with him allowed to join her and me to remain as housekeeper. It seemed almost too favourable an arrangement to hope for. Yet I did hope, and began to take comfort in the prospect of keeping my home and work, and above all my beloved young mistress. Just then a servant, one of those dismissed but not yet gone, rushed in to say “that devil Heathcliff” was crossing the yard. Should he shut the door in his face?

Even if we had been mad enough to order that, there was no time. He did not trouble to knock or announce himself. He was the master and used the master's privilege of walking straight in without a word. The servant's voice led him to the library. He entered, motioned the man out, and shut the door.

It was the same room into which he had been shown as a guest eighteen years earlier. The same moon shone through the window, and the same autumn landscape lay outside. We had not yet lit a candle, but the whole room was visible, including the portraits on the wall: Mrs. Linton's magnificent head and her husband's graceful one. Heathcliff walked towards the hearth. Time had changed his appearance very little either. He was the same man, his dark face a little more sallow and composed, his body perhaps a stone or two heavier, but otherwise unchanged. At the sight of him, Catherine had jumped up, meaning to rush out.

“Stop!” he said, catching her arm. “No more running away! Where would you go? I've come to take you home. I hope you'll be a dutiful daughter and won't encourage my son to disobey me again. When I discovered his part in the affair, I hardly knew how to punish him. He's such a cobweb that a pinch would destroy him. But you'll see from his face that he's had his due! The evening before last I brought him downstairs and put him in a chair, and didn't touch him afterwards. I sent Hareton out, so we had the room to ourselves. Two hours later I called Joseph to carry him upstairs again. Since then my presence has affected his nerves as powerfully as a ghost, and I fancy he often sees me when I'm nowhere near. Hareton says he wakes and screams for hours in the night, calling for you to protect him from me. Whether you like your precious husband or not, you must come. He's your responsibility now. I hand over all my concern in him to you.”
“Why not let Catherine stay here,” I pleaded, “and send Master Linton to her? Since you hate them both, you wouldn't miss them. They _must_ be a daily nuisance to that unnatural heart of yours.”

“I'm looking for a tenant for the Grange,” he answered, “and of course I want my children around me. Besides, the girl owes me work for her keep. I'm not going to support her in idleness and luxury after Linton's gone. Hurry up and get ready, now. Don't make me force you.”

“I will,” Catherine said. “Linton is all I have left in the world to love. You've done everything you could to make me hate him and him hate me, but you _can't_ make us hate each other. And I defy you to hurt him while I'm there. I defy you to frighten me!”

“What a boastful defender you are,” Heathcliff replied. “But I don't like you enough to hurt him. You'll have the full benefit of that torment for as long as it lasts. I won't be the one who makes you hate him: his own sweet nature will do that. He's bitter as gall about your desertion and its consequences. Don't expect thanks for this noble devotion. I heard him painting Zillah a pretty picture of what he'd do if he were as strong as me. The will is there, and his very weakness will sharpen his wits to find something to replace strength.”

“I know his nature is bad,” Catherine said. “He's your son. But I'm glad mine is better, so I can forgive it. I know he loves me, and that's why I love him. Mr. Heathcliff, _you_ have _no one_ who loves you. However miserable you make us, we'll still have the revenge of knowing your cruelty comes from being even more miserable yourself. You _are_ miserable, aren't you? Lonely as the devil, and envious like him? _Nobody_ loves you. _Nobody_ will cry when you die! I wouldn't be you!”
She spoke with a bleak sort of triumph. It seemed she had resolved to adopt the spirit of the family she was joining and find pleasure in her enemies' suffering.
“You'll soon be sorry to be yourself,” her father-in-law said, “if you stand there a minute longer. Off with you, witch! Get your things!”

She left with a look of contempt. While she was gone, I began begging to take Zillah's place at the Heights, offering to give up mine to her. He would not hear of it. He ordered me to be quiet, then for the first time let his eyes travel around the room and over the portraits. After studying Mrs. Linton's, he said, “I'll have that taken home. Not that I need it, but—” He turned sharply towards the fire and continued with what, for want of a better word, I must call a smile. “I'll tell you what I did yesterday. The sexton was digging Linton's grave. I got him to clear the earth from her coffin lid, and I opened it. For a moment I thought I'd stay there. When I saw her face again—it's still her face!—he could hardly move me. But he said it would change if the air reached it, so I loosened one side of the coffin and covered it up. Not the side nearest Linton, damn him! I wish he'd been sealed in lead. I bribed the sexton to pull that side away when I'm buried there and slide mine out too—I'll have my coffin made that way. Then by the time Linton reaches us, he won't know which is which!”
“That was very wicked, Mr. Heathcliff!” I exclaimed. “Weren't you ashamed to disturb the dead?”

“I disturbed no one, Nelly,” he replied, “and I brought myself some peace. I'll be much more comfortable now, and you'll have a better chance of keeping me underground once I'm there. Disturb her? No! She's disturbed me, day and night, for eighteen years—without rest, without mercy—until last night. Last night I was at peace. I dreamt I was sleeping my last sleep beside her, my heart stopped and my cheek frozen against hers.”
“And if she'd crumbled into earth, or something worse, what would you have dreamt then?” I asked.

“Of crumbling with her, and being happier still!” he answered. “Do you think I fear any change like that? I expected it when I lifted the lid, but I'm better pleased that it should wait until I can share it. Besides, without that clear impression of her still, untroubled features, I could hardly have shaken off that strange feeling. It began in an odd way. You know how wild I was after her death, praying without end, from dawn to dawn, for her spirit to return to me! I believe strongly in ghosts. I'm convinced they can exist among us, and do! Snow fell on the day she was buried. That evening I went to the churchyard. The wind was bleak as winter, and the place was deserted. I wasn't afraid her fool of a husband would wander up the valley so late, and no one else had any reason to be there. Alone, knowing that only two yards of loose earth stood between us, I said to myself, ‘I'll hold her in my arms again! If she's cold, I'll think it's this north wind chilling _me_. If she doesn't move, she's asleep.’ I fetched a spade from the tool shed and dug with all my strength. It scraped the coffin. I began working with my hands, and the wood started cracking around the screws. I was just about to succeed when I seemed to hear someone sigh above me, bending down close to the edge of the grave. ‘If only I can get this off,’ I muttered, ‘let them shovel the earth over both of us!’ I wrenched at it more desperately than ever. Another sigh came close to my ear. I seemed to feel its warm breath push aside the sleet-filled wind. I knew no living person of flesh and blood was there. But as surely as you sense yourself approaching a solid object in the dark without being able to see it, I felt Cathy there—not beneath me, but above ground. Relief suddenly flowed from my heart through every limb. I abandoned that agonising labour and turned away, instantly comforted—comforted beyond words. Her presence stayed with me while I filled in the grave, and led me home. Laugh if you like, but I was certain I'd see her there. I knew she was with me and couldn't help speaking to her. When I reached the Heights, I rushed eagerly to the door. It was locked. I remember that accursed Earnshaw and my wife trying to keep me out. I remember stopping to kick the breath out of him, then hurrying upstairs to the room that had been mine and hers. I looked impatiently around. I felt her beside me. I could _almost_ see her, and yet I _could not_! I should have sweated blood then from the agony of longing, from the desperate force of my prayers for just one glimpse. I got none. She proved herself a devil to me, as she so often had in life! Since then, more at some times and less at others, I've been the plaything of that unbearable torture. Hellish! It has kept my nerves stretched so tight that, if they hadn't been made of catgut, they would long ago have gone as slack and feeble as Linton's. Sitting in the house with Hareton, I'd feel that if I went out I'd meet her. Walking on the moors, I'd feel I'd meet her when I came in. Whenever I left home I hurried back. She _must_ be somewhere at the Heights; I was certain of it! As for sleeping in her room—I was driven out of that. I couldn't lie there. The moment I closed my eyes she was outside the window, or pushing back the panels, or coming through the door, or even resting her darling head on the same pillow as she used to as a child. I had to open my eyes and look. So I opened and closed them a hundred times a night, always to be disappointed! It tortured me! I've often groaned aloud until that old scoundrel Joseph must have thought my conscience was playing the devil inside me. Now that I've seen her, I'm calmer—a little. What a strange way to kill a man: not by inches, but by fractions of a hair's breadth, luring me on with the ghost of a hope for eighteen years!”

Mr. Heathcliff stopped and wiped his forehead, where his hair clung wet with sweat. His eyes were fixed on the red embers. His eyebrows were not drawn together but raised towards the temples, making his face less grim, yet giving it a peculiar troubled look, a painful appearance of a mind strained towards one all-consuming subject. He was only half speaking to me, and I kept quiet. I did not like hearing him talk! After a short while he returned his attention to the portrait, took it down, and leaned it against the sofa to see it better. While he was occupied with it, Catherine came in and announced that she was ready as soon as her pony was saddled.

“Send that over tomorrow,” Heathcliff told me. Then he turned to her. “You can do without the pony. It's a fine evening, and you won't need ponies at Wuthering Heights. Your own feet will do for any journeys you make. Come along.”
“Goodbye, Ellen,” my dear little mistress whispered. Her lips were icy as she kissed me. “Come and see me, Ellen. Don't forget.”
“Make sure you do nothing of the sort, Mrs. Dean!” said her new father. “When I want to speak to you, I'll come here. I don't want you prying around my house!”

He motioned her ahead of him. With a backward look that cut me to the heart, she obeyed. From the window I watched them go down the garden. Heathcliff tucked Catherine's arm under his, though she clearly resisted at first, and hurried her with long strides into the avenue, where the trees hid them from sight.

chapters.title: Chapter XXX
paragraphs: I have been to the Heights, but I have not seen her since she left. When I called to ask about her, Joseph held the door and would not let me in. He said Mrs. Linton was “busy” and the master was out. Zillah has told me something of their life there; otherwise I would scarcely know who was alive and who was dead. From the way she talks, I gather that she thinks Catherine proud and dislikes her. When my young mistress first arrived, she asked Zillah for help, but Mr. Heathcliff told the woman to mind her own business and let his daughter-in-law look after herself. Zillah, being narrow-minded and selfish, was quite willing to obey. Catherine resented this neglect like a child and answered it with contempt, making an enemy of my informant as surely as if she had done her some terrible injury. About six weeks ago, shortly before you came, I met Zillah on the moor and had a long talk with her. This is what she told me.

“The first thing Mrs. Linton did when she reached the Heights,” she said, “was run upstairs without even saying good evening to me or Joseph. She shut herself in Linton's room and stayed there until morning. Then, while the master and Earnshaw were having breakfast, she came down into the main room, trembling all over, and asked if we could send for the doctor. Her cousin was very ill.
“‘We know that!’ Heathcliff answered. ‘But his life isn't worth a farthing, and I won't spend a farthing on him.’
“‘But I don't know what to do,’ she said. ‘If nobody helps me, he'll die!’
“‘Get out of this room,’ the master cried, ‘and don't let me hear another word about him! Nobody here cares what happens to him. If you care, nurse him. If you don't, lock him up and leave him.’

“Then she started bothering me. I told her I'd had enough trouble with the tiresome creature. We each had our work, and hers was to look after Linton. Mr. Heathcliff had told me to leave that job to her.

“I can't say how they managed together. I imagine he fretted a great deal and lay groaning day and night, and she got precious little rest. You could tell from her white face and heavy eyes. Sometimes she came into the kitchen looking quite bewildered, as though she wanted to beg for help. But I wasn't going to disobey the master. I never dare disobey him, Mrs. Dean. Though I thought it wrong not to send for Kenneth, it wasn't my place to advise or complain, and I always refused to interfere. Once or twice, after we'd gone to bed, I happened to open my door and see her sitting at the top of the stairs crying. Then I shut myself in quickly, for fear I'd be moved to do something. I did feel sorry for her then, certainly. Still, I didn't want to lose my position, you understand.
“At last, one night she walked straight into my room and frightened me out of my wits by saying, ‘Tell Mr. Heathcliff his son is dying. I'm certain of it this time. Get up at once and tell him.’
“Then she disappeared again. I lay there listening and trembling for a quarter of an hour. Nothing moved. The house was silent.

“She's mistaken, I told myself. He's recovered. There's no need to disturb them. I began to doze, but a sharp ringing of the bell woke me again—the only bell we have, installed specially for Linton. The master called to me to find out what was wrong and tell them he wouldn't have that noise again.

“I gave him Catherine's message. He swore to himself, and a few minutes later came out with a lighted candle and went to their room. I followed him. Mrs. Heathcliff sat beside the bed with her hands folded on her knees. Her father-in-law approached, held the candle to Linton's face, looked at him and touched him, then turned to her.
“‘Well, Catherine,’ he said, ‘how do you feel?’
“She said nothing.
“‘How do you feel, Catherine?’ he asked again.

“‘He's safe, and I'm free,’ she answered. ‘I ought to feel well. But’—she couldn't hide her bitterness—‘you've left me struggling alone against death so long that death is all I can see or feel! I feel like death!’

“And she looked like it! I gave her a little wine. Hareton and Joseph had been woken by the bell and footsteps and had heard us talking from outside; now they came in. I think Joseph was pleased to be rid of the boy. Hareton looked a little troubled, though he was more occupied with staring at Catherine than thinking about Linton. The master told him to go back to bed: we didn't need his help. Afterwards he made Joseph carry the body to his own room and told me to go back to mine, leaving Mrs. Heathcliff alone.

“In the morning he sent me to tell her to come down for breakfast. She'd undressed and seemed about to sleep. She said she was ill, which hardly surprised me. I told Mr. Heathcliff, and he said, ‘Well, leave her alone until after the funeral. Go up now and then and bring her what she needs. Tell me as soon as she seems better.’”

According to Zillah, Cathy stayed upstairs for a fortnight. Zillah visited twice a day and would have been somewhat friendlier, but every attempt at greater kindness was immediately and proudly rejected.

Heathcliff went up once to show her Linton's will. He had left his father all his own movable property and everything of that kind which had formerly been hers. The poor creature had been threatened or coaxed into doing it during the week she was away, when his uncle died. Being under age, he could not dispose of the land. Yet Mr. Heathcliff has claimed and kept it through his wife's rights and his own—legally, I suppose. At any rate Catherine, with no money and no friends, cannot challenge his possession.

“Except for that one time,” Zillah said, “I was the only person who ever came to her door, and nobody asked about her. She first came down into the main room on a Sunday afternoon. When I took up her dinner, she'd cried out that she couldn't bear the cold any longer. I told her the master was going to Thrushcross Grange, and Earnshaw and I needn't stop her coming downstairs. So as soon as she heard Heathcliff's horse trot away, she appeared. She was dressed in black, with her yellow curls combed back behind her ears as plainly as a Quaker's. She couldn't comb the curl out of them.

“Joseph and I generally go to chapel on Sundays”—the church has no minister now, Mrs. Dean explained; they call the Methodist or Baptist place in Gimmerton a chapel, I couldn't tell you which it is—“and Joseph had gone,” she continued, “but I thought it best to stay at home. Young people are always better with an older person watching them, and for all his shyness, Hareton isn't a model of good manners. I told him his cousin would probably sit with us, and that she was used to seeing the Sabbath respected. He'd better leave his guns and indoor jobs alone while she was there. He went red at the news and looked down at his hands and clothes. The whale oil and gunpowder disappeared in a moment. I saw he meant to keep her company, and guessed from his manner that he wanted to look presentable. So I laughed, as I wouldn't dare with the master there, offered to help him if he liked, and teased him about his embarrassment. He turned sulky and began swearing.

“Now, Mrs. Dean,” Zillah went on, seeing that her manner displeased me, “perhaps you think your young lady too fine for Mr. Hareton. Perhaps you're right. But I admit I'd be glad to see her pride brought down a peg. What good will all her learning and fine ways do her now? She's as poor as you or me—poorer, I'll wager. You're saving, and I'm doing my little bit that way too.”

Hareton let Zillah help him, and her flattery put him in a good humour. So when Catherine appeared, he partly forgot her earlier insults and tried, according to the housekeeper, to make himself agreeable.

“The mistress walked in,” she said, “cold as an icicle and proud as a princess. I stood up and offered her my armchair. No—she turned up her nose at my kindness. Earnshaw stood too and invited her to sit on the settle close to the fire. He said she must be frozen.
“‘I've been frozen for a month and more,’ she answered, putting all the contempt she could into the word.

“She fetched her own chair and set it away from both of us. After she'd sat long enough to warm up, she looked around and noticed some books on the dresser. At once she stood and reached for them, but they were too high. Her cousin watched her trying for a while, then at last found the courage to help. She held out her skirt, and he filled it with the first books he could reach.

“That was a great step forward for the lad. She didn't thank him, but he was pleased that she'd accepted his help. He ventured to stand behind her while she looked through them, even bending down to point out things he liked in some of the old pictures. The rude way she jerked the page away from his finger didn't discourage him. He merely moved back a little and looked at her instead of the book. She went on reading, or looking for something to read. Gradually all his attention settled on her thick, silky curls. He couldn't see her face, and she couldn't see him. Perhaps without quite knowing what he was doing, drawn like a child to a candle, he finally went from looking to touching. He reached out and stroked one curl as gently as if it were a bird. You'd have thought he'd stuck a knife in her neck, the way she spun around in a fury.
“‘Go away this instant! How dare you touch me? Why are you standing there?’ she cried in disgust. ‘I can't bear you! If you come near me, I'll go upstairs again.’

“Mr. Hareton drew back, looking as foolish as could be, and sat very quietly on the settle. She went on turning through her books for another half-hour. At last Earnshaw came over and whispered to me.
“‘Will ye ask her to read to us, Zillah? I'm tired of doing nowt, and I do like—I would like to hear her! Don't say I asked. Ask her for thysen.’
“‘Mr. Hareton would like you to read to us, ma'am,’ I said at once. ‘He'd think it very kind. He'd be much obliged.’
“She frowned, looked up, and answered—

“‘Mr. Hareton, and all the rest of you, will kindly understand that I reject every sham kindness you're hypocritical enough to offer! I despise you and want nothing to do with any of you! When I'd have given my life for one kind word, even the sight of one of your faces, you all stayed away. But I won't complain to you. The cold has driven me down here. I haven't come to entertain you or enjoy your company.’
“‘What could I have done?’ Earnshaw began. ‘How was I to blame?’
“‘Oh, you're an exception,’ Mrs. Heathcliff replied. ‘I never missed anything like you.’
“‘But I offered more than once, and I asked,’ he said, growing angry at her insolence. ‘I asked Mr. Heathcliff to let me sit up for you—’
“‘Be quiet! I'll go outside, or anywhere at all, rather than listen to that horrible voice of yours!’ my lady said.

“Hareton muttered that she could go to hell for all he cared. He took down his gun and no longer held back from his Sunday occupations. He talked freely enough now, and before long she chose to retreat to her solitude. But the frost had arrived, and despite her pride she had to stoop to joining us more and more often. I made sure she had no further chance to sneer at my kindness. Ever since then I've been as cold as she is. Nobody here loves her or likes her, and she doesn't deserve it. Let anyone say the least thing to her and she bristles, with no respect for anyone. She'll snap even at the master, almost daring him to beat her, and the more she's hurt, the more spiteful she becomes.”

When Zillah first told me this, I resolved to leave my position, take a cottage, and persuade Catherine to live with me. But Mr. Heathcliff would no more allow that than he would set Hareton up in a house of his own. At present I can see no way out unless she marries again, and that is not something I have the power to arrange.

So Mrs. Dean's story ended. Despite the doctor's prediction, I am rapidly regaining my strength. Though it is only the second week of January, I mean to get out on horseback in a day or two and ride to Wuthering Heights. I shall tell my landlord that I intend to spend the next six months in London, and that he may, if he wishes, find another tenant to take the house after October. Nothing short of a great reward would make me spend another winter here.

chapters.title: Chapter XXXI
paragraphs: Yesterday was clear, still, and frosty. I went to the Heights as planned. My housekeeper begged me to carry a short note to her young mistress, and I agreed, since the good woman saw nothing odd in the request. The front door stood open, but the unwelcoming gate was locked, as on my previous visit. I knocked, calling Earnshaw away from the garden beds. He unfastened the chain and let me in. The fellow is as handsome a countryman as one could wish to see. I noticed him particularly this time, though he seems determined to make as little as possible of his advantages.

I asked whether Mr. Heathcliff was home. He said no, but he would return for dinner. It was eleven o'clock. When I said I would go in and wait, he immediately put down his tools and came with me, acting as a watchdog rather than a substitute host.

We went in together. Catherine was there, making herself useful by preparing vegetables for the coming meal. She looked sulkier and less spirited than when I first saw her. She barely raised her eyes at my arrival and continued her task with the same disregard for ordinary politeness as before, offering not the slightest acknowledgment of my bow or good morning.
“She doesn't seem as pleasant as Mrs. Dean would have me believe,” I thought. “A beauty, certainly, but no angel.”

Earnshaw gruffly told her to take her things into the kitchen. “Take them yourself,” she said, pushing them away as soon as she had finished. She withdrew to a stool by the window and began cutting shapes of birds and animals from the turnip peelings in her lap. Pretending I wanted to look at the garden, I approached and, very deftly I thought, dropped Mrs. Dean's note onto her knee without Hareton noticing. But she asked aloud, “What's that?” and tossed it off.

“A letter from your old friend, the housekeeper at the Grange,” I answered, annoyed that she had exposed my kindness and afraid it might be mistaken for a message of my own. On hearing this she would gladly have picked it up, but Hareton was quicker. He snatched it and put it inside his waistcoat, saying Mr. Heathcliff must see it first. Catherine silently turned away from us, slipped out her handkerchief as secretly as she could, and put it to her eyes. For a while her cousin struggled to suppress his softer feelings, then pulled out the letter and threw it on the floor beside her as ungraciously as possible. Catherine seized it and read it eagerly. She asked me a few questions about the inhabitants of her former home, human and animal, then looked towards the hills and murmured to herself:

“I wish I could ride Minny down there! I wish I could climb up there! Oh, I'm tired—I'm _fed up_, Hareton!” She leaned her pretty head against the sill with a sound halfway between a yawn and a sigh, and sank into an absent sadness, neither knowing nor caring whether we noticed her.

“Mrs. Heathcliff,” I said after sitting silently for some time, “do you realise that I know you? So well, in fact, that I'm surprised you won't come and talk to me. My housekeeper never tires of talking about you and singing your praises. She'll be terribly disappointed if I bring back no news of you, or message from you, beyond saying that you received her letter and said nothing!”
She seemed surprised by this speech and asked—
“Does Ellen like you?”
“Yes, very much,” I answered, with some hesitation.
“Then tell her,” she continued, “that I'd answer her letter, but I've nothing to write with or on. Not even a book I could tear a page from.”
“No books!” I exclaimed. “If I may ask, how do you manage to live here without them? Even with a large library, I'm often terribly bored at the Grange. Take my books away and I'd be desperate!”

“When I had them, I was always reading,” Catherine said. “Mr. Heathcliff never reads, so he took it into his head to destroy my books. I haven't seen one for weeks. Once I searched through Joseph's stock of theology, which made him furious. And once, Hareton, I found a secret collection in your room: Latin and Greek, stories and poetry, all old friends. The stories and poems were ones I'd brought here. You collected them like a magpie collecting silver spoons, simply for the pleasure of stealing! They're no use to you. Or perhaps you hid them out of spite: if you can't enjoy them, nobody else shall. Perhaps it was _your_ envy that suggested Mr. Heathcliff should rob me of my treasures? But most of them are written in my mind and printed on my heart, and you can't take those away!”
Earnshaw went crimson as his cousin exposed his private collection of books and stammered an indignant denial of her charges.
“Mr. Hareton wishes to improve his knowledge,” I said, coming to his aid. “He doesn't _envy_ your accomplishments; he wants to _equal_ them. In a few years he'll be a fine scholar.”

“And meanwhile he wants me to become a dunce,” Catherine replied. “Yes, I hear him trying to spell and read to himself. What fine mistakes he makes! I wish you'd repeat Chevy Chase the way you did yesterday. It was extremely funny. I heard you, and I heard you searching the dictionary for the difficult words, then swearing because you couldn't read the definitions!”

The young man plainly thought it unfair to be mocked for his ignorance, then mocked again for trying to overcome it. I thought much the same. Remembering Mrs. Dean's account of his first attempt to dispel the darkness in which he had been raised, I remarked, “But, Mrs. Heathcliff, we all had to begin, and we all stumbled and faltered at first. If our teachers had mocked us instead of helping, we'd still be stumbling and faltering.”

“Oh, I don't want to limit his learning,” she replied. “But he has no right to take what's mine and make it ridiculous to me with his horrible mistakes and mispronunciations! Those books, the prose and the poetry alike, are sacred to me because of other memories. I hate hearing them degraded and profaned in his mouth! And out of everything he could choose, he's picked my favourite passages, the ones I most love to repeat, as though deliberately to spite me.”

For a minute Hareton's chest heaved in silence. His humiliation and anger were intense, and he struggled to control them. With a gentleman's wish to ease his embarrassment, I got up and stood in the doorway, looking outside. He followed my example and left the room, but soon returned with half a dozen books. He flung them into Catherine's lap, exclaiming, “Take them! I never want to hear them, read them, or think of them again!”
“I don't want them now,” she answered. “They'll remind me of you, and I'll hate them.”

She opened one that had clearly been much handled and read a passage in a beginner's slow, dragging voice. Then she laughed and threw it away. “And listen to this,” she went on tauntingly, beginning a verse of an old ballad in the same manner.

But his pride could bear no more torment. I heard a blow silence her insolent tongue, and I did not entirely disapprove. The little wretch had done everything she could to wound her cousin's sensitive, though uncultivated, feelings. Physical force was the only argument he had to settle the account and return some of the hurt to the person who had inflicted it. Afterwards he gathered the books and threw them into the fire. His face showed the anguish of that sacrifice to anger. As they burned, I imagined him remembering the pleasure they had already given him, and the triumph and ever greater pleasures he had expected from them. I thought I could also guess what had prompted his secret studies. Until Catherine crossed his path, he had been content with daily labour and coarse, physical pleasures. Shame at her contempt and hope of winning her approval had first stirred him towards higher things. Instead of protecting him from the first and winning him the second, his efforts to improve himself had achieved precisely the opposite.
“Yes, that's all a brute like you can get out of them!” Catherine cried, sucking her injured lip and watching the blaze with angry eyes.
“You'd _better_ keep quiet now,” he answered fiercely.

He was too agitated to say more. He hurried towards the doorway, where I stepped aside for him. But before he had crossed the threshold, Mr. Heathcliff met him coming up the paved path, laid a hand on his shoulder, and asked, “What's the matter now, lad?”
“Nowt, nowt,” he said, breaking away to indulge his grief and anger alone.
Heathcliff watched him go and sighed.

“It would be strange if I defeated myself,” he muttered, unaware that I stood behind him. “But when I look for his father in his face, I find more of _her_ every day! How the devil can he be so like her? I can hardly bear to look at him.”

He lowered his eyes and went gloomily inside. His face had a restless, anxious expression I had never seen before, and he looked thinner. His daughter-in-law had spotted him through the window and immediately escaped to the kitchen, leaving me alone.

“I'm glad to see you out again, Mr. Lockwood,” he said in answer to my greeting. “Partly for selfish reasons. In this wilderness I don't think I could easily find someone to replace you. More than once I've wondered what brought you here.”

“An idle whim, I'm afraid, sir,” I replied. “Or else it's an idle whim that's about to carry me away. I leave for London next week, and I must warn you that I have no wish to keep Thrushcross Grange beyond the twelve months I agreed to rent it. I don't think I shall live there again.”

“Indeed! Tired of exile from the world, are you?” he said. “But if you've come to ask to be excused from paying for a house you won't occupy, you've wasted your journey. I never let anyone off what they owe me.”
“I've come to ask for no such thing!” I exclaimed, thoroughly irritated. “If you wish, I'll settle with you now.” I took my notebook from my pocket.

“No, no,” he replied coolly. “If you don't come back, you'll leave enough behind to cover your debts. I'm in no hurry. Sit down and have dinner with us. A guest who can be relied on not to return is generally welcome. Catherine! Bring the things in. Where are you?”
Catherine came back carrying a tray of knives and forks.
“You can eat with Joseph,” Heathcliff muttered to her aside, “and stay in the kitchen until he's gone.”
She followed his instructions exactly. Perhaps she felt no temptation to disobey. Living among boors and people who hate mankind, she probably cannot appreciate better company when she encounters it.

With Mr. Heathcliff grim and gloomy on one side and Hareton entirely silent on the other, I ate a rather cheerless meal and took my leave early. I would have gone out the back way for a final glimpse of Catherine and the pleasure of annoying old Joseph. But Hareton was told to bring my horse round, and my host himself escorted me to the front door, thwarting my intention.

“How drearily life passes in that house!” I reflected as I rode down the road. “What a fulfilment of something more romantic than a fairy tale it would have been for Mrs. Linton Heathcliff if she and I had fallen in love, as her good nurse wished, and gone off together into the lively atmosphere of town!”

chapters.title: Chapter XXXII
paragraphs: 1802.—This September a friend in the north invited me to help devastate the game on his moors. On my way to his house, I unexpectedly found myself within fifteen miles of Gimmerton. At a roadside inn, the stableman was holding a bucket of water for my horses when a cart passed laden with newly cut oats, still very green. “That's from Gimmerton,” he remarked. “They're always three weeks behind other folk with their harvest.”
“Gimmerton?” I repeated. My time in that neighbourhood already seemed dim and dreamlike. “Ah, yes. How far is it from here?”
“Maybe fourteen miles over t' hills,” he answered. “And a rough road.”

I suddenly felt an urge to visit Thrushcross Grange. It was barely noon, and I thought I might as well sleep under my own roof as at an inn. Besides, I could easily spare a day to settle matters with my landlord and save myself another journey into the neighbourhood. After resting a while, I told my servant to ask the way to the village. We covered the distance in about three hours, greatly tiring our horses.

I left him there and went on alone down the valley. The grey church looked greyer, the lonely churchyard lonelier. I saw a moorland sheep cropping the short grass on the graves. The weather was lovely and warm—too warm for travelling—but the heat did not spoil my pleasure in the beautiful scenery above and below. Had I seen it nearer August, I am sure it would have tempted me to idle away a month in those solitary places. Nothing could be drearier in winter, or more heavenly in summer, than those valleys enclosed by hills and those bold, steep swells of heather.

I reached the Grange before sunset and knocked. But a single thin curl of blue smoke rising from the kitchen chimney suggested that the household had withdrawn to the back, and no one heard me. I rode into the yard. A girl of nine or ten sat knitting under the porch, while an old woman reclined on the steps, thoughtfully smoking a pipe.
“Is Mrs. Dean in?” I asked the old woman.
“Mistress Dean? Nay!” she answered. “She doesn't live here. She's up at t' Heights.”
“Then are you the housekeeper?” I asked.
“Aye, I keep t' house,” she replied.
“Well, I'm Mr. Lockwood, the master. I wonder whether there's a room for me? I'd like to stay the night.”
“T' master!” she cried in amazement. “Why, who knew ye were coming? Ye should have sent word. There's nowt dry or decent about t' place—not a thing!”

She dropped her pipe and hurried inside, followed by the girl and then me. I soon saw that her description was accurate and that my unwelcome appearance had almost driven her out of her wits. I told her to calm herself. I would go for a walk; meanwhile she should try to prepare a corner of a sitting room for my supper and a bedroom for the night. There was no need to sweep or dust: a good fire and dry sheets would be enough. She seemed eager to do her best, though she thrust the hearth brush into the grate instead of the poker and put several other tools to equally unsuitable uses. I left, trusting her energy to provide somewhere to rest on my return. Wuthering Heights was my destination. Just after leaving the yard, another thought brought me back.
“Is everyone well at the Heights?” I asked her.
“Aye, for all I know!” she answered, hurrying away with a pan of hot cinders.

I wanted to ask why Mrs. Dean had left the Grange, but at such a crisis I could not detain the woman, so I turned and went. I walked at leisure, with the glow of the setting sun behind me and the gentle splendour of the rising moon ahead, one fading as the other brightened. Leaving the park, I climbed the stony side road to Mr. Heathcliff's house. Before it came into sight, all that remained of daylight was a flat amber glow in the west. Yet the magnificent moon showed every pebble in the path and every blade of grass. I had neither to climb the gate nor knock: it opened at my touch. An improvement, I thought. My nose discovered another: the fragrance of stocks and wallflowers drifted through the air from among the familiar fruit trees.

The doors and windows were open, yet a fine red fire lit the hearth, as is usual in a coal district. The comfort of the sight makes the extra heat bearable. Besides, the main room at Wuthering Heights is large enough for its occupants to sit well beyond the fire's warmth. Those present had accordingly settled near a window. Before entering I could see them and hear their conversation, and so I watched and listened, drawn by a mixture of curiosity and envy that grew the longer I lingered.
“Con-_trary_!” said a voice sweet as a silver bell. “That's the third time, you dunce! I won't tell you again. Remember, or I'll pull your hair!”
“Contrary, then,” another voice answered, deep but gentle. “Now kiss me for getting it right.”
“No. Read it through correctly first, without one mistake.”

The young man began reading. He was respectably dressed and seated at a table with a book before him. His handsome face glowed with pleasure, and his eyes kept straying impatiently from the page to a small white hand over his shoulder. Whenever its owner caught these signs of inattention, a brisk slap on his cheek brought him back to his work. She stood behind him, her bright, fair ringlets sometimes mingling with his brown hair as she bent over to guide his studies. Her face—it was fortunate he could not see her face, or he would never have stayed so attentive. I could see it, and bit my lip with resentment at having thrown away whatever chance I might once have had to do more than stare at its devastating beauty.

The lesson ended, though not without further mistakes. The pupil claimed his reward and received at least five kisses, which he generously returned. Then they came to the door. From their conversation I gathered that they meant to walk on the moors. I supposed Hareton Earnshaw would condemn me, inwardly if not aloud, to the deepest pit of hell if I showed my unfortunate face near him just then. Feeling thoroughly small and spiteful, I slunk round to seek refuge in the kitchen. That entrance was open too. By the door sat my old friend Nelly Dean, sewing and singing, though her song was repeatedly interrupted from inside by harsh expressions of contempt and intolerance delivered in a far from musical voice.

“I'd far rather have them swearing in my ears from morning till night than listen to thee at all!” said the occupant of the kitchen, answering something I had not heard Nelly say. “It's a blazing shame I can't open t' blessed Book without thee starting up those praises of Satan and all t' dreadful wickedness ever born into this world! Oh, thou's a right good-for-nowt, and so is she, and that poor lad'll be lost between ye. Poor lad!” he added with a groan. “He's bewitched, I'm certain of it. Oh, Lord, judge them, for there's neither law nor justice among our rulers!”

“No, or I suppose we'd be sitting in burning bundles of sticks,” the singer retorted. “But hush, old man. Read your Bible like a Christian and leave me alone. This is ‘Fairy Annie's Wedding,’ a lovely tune, and you can dance to it.”

Mrs. Dean was about to begin again when I stepped forward. Recognising me at once, she sprang up. “Why, bless you, Mr. Lockwood! How could you think of coming back like this? Thrushcross Grange is all shut up. You should have let us know!”
“I've arranged to stay there for as long as I need,” I replied. “I leave again tomorrow. But how did you come to be transplanted here, Mrs. Dean? Tell me that.”
“Zillah left, and soon after you went to London Mr. Heathcliff asked me to come and stay until you returned. But do come in! Have you walked from Gimmerton this evening?”
“From the Grange,” I answered. “While they make a room ready for me, I want to finish my business with your master. I don't expect another opportunity soon.”
“What business, sir?” Nelly asked, leading me inside. “He's out at the moment and won't be back for a while.”
“The rent,” I answered.
“Oh! Then you'll have to settle that with Mrs. Heathcliff,” she said, “or rather with me. She hasn't learnt to manage her affairs yet, so I act for her. There's no one else.”
I looked surprised.
“Ah, I see you haven't heard of Heathcliff's death,” she continued.
“Heathcliff dead!” I exclaimed in astonishment. “How long ago?”
“Three months. But sit down and give me your hat, and I'll tell you everything. Wait—you haven't had anything to eat, have you?”
“I don't need anything. I've ordered supper at home. Sit down yourself. I never imagined he'd die! Tell me how it happened. You say they won't be back for some time—the young people?”
“No. I have to scold them every evening for walking out so late, but they take no notice of me. At least have some of our old ale. It'll do you good; you look tired.”

She hurried to fetch it before I could refuse. I heard Joseph asking whether “it wasn't a crying scandal for her to have men following her at her age? And then to fetch those jugs out of t' master's cellar! He was fair ashamed to stand by and watch it.”

She did not pause to answer him, but returned a moment later with a silver pint mug foaming at the brim. I praised its contents with appropriate enthusiasm. Then she told me the rest of Heathcliff's story. He had come to a “queer” end, as she put it.

Within a fortnight of your departure, she said, I was summoned to Wuthering Heights, and for Catherine's sake I went gladly. My first meeting with her shocked and grieved me: she had changed so much since we parted. Mr. Heathcliff gave no reason for changing his mind about my coming. He merely said he wanted me and was tired of seeing Catherine. I was to use the little parlour as my sitting room and keep her with me. Having to see her once or twice a day was enough for him.
